Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Jason Bell wrote:
>
> "James Coupe" <ja...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote

> price/booster size, or perhaps more, depending on demand
> for individual title), or at the very least in complete sets
> (at [set size/booster size]*booster price).

...

> Of course we're being fleeced.

We are being "fleeced" if that's how you want to define it. The
question isn't how they're making money, it's just the price they
want to set on the product. In the world of randomly packed boosters
with a rarity-level curve, the "price" is set by the degree of rarity
that the rarest cards have in relation to the most common cards.
Along with, of course, the traditional pricing question of how much
they charge for a pack of how many cards.

I believe, in this case, that it was not intentional on White Wolf's
part to create super-expensive super-rare cards. And it's not yet
clear that that's what will happen in the long run WRT to the R1s in
Final Nights. (I have my opinion about it but I'm just guessing
based on past experience which may or may not prove to be valid.)
But some of the comments that Scott made about rare cards leads me
to suspect some naivety on WW's part about what kinds of rarity formats
will lead to what results. One problem with the CCG industry is that
all the important decisions often get made by people who don't necessarily
know what it feels like to collect, trade, and buy for real life
card collections.

While we're on the subject, by the way, I have the same opinion about
the single new vampire in each starter, precon deck printed by Final
Nights. Is it just me or is anyone else frustrated about this? Without
this single new vampire, the only reason a person who had an adequate (what
he felt was adequate) collection of older cards now has this one single
card that he wands from the starter decks. This, IMO, was the absolute
*WORST* thing they could have done. Had they peppered the whole starter
deck with new stuff, then we'd have to buy the starter decks to get the new
stuff but at least we'd be getting lots of new stuff. As it is, if we
want the new vampire, we have have to buy the starter deck to get it,
one per whole deck, and the rest of the stuff doesn't add anything to
our collections. Not entirely, of course - some reprints will likely
add to most everyone's collections. You get Dreams with the Giovanni
deck, lots of rare Settite stuff with the Settite deck, and so forth.
But you know what I mean. It's frustrating that they pledged to put
only reprints in the starter deck and then couldn't resist sticking *one*
new vampire, and thus wound up falling through the cracks and not doing
either of the two more sensible extremes. Arg!

Fred

Messages.Author: Ian Lee
Messages.Body:
>>And, why bother having R1s at all (ignoring that it
>>is a sales gimmick)?
>
>Bing bing bing bing bing.
>
>White Wolf are not out to fleece us, but they do want to make money.

I've been through this with another company. Sure, at the high end, you
encourage the Mr. Suitcases to get a significant number of additional cards.
OTOH, there's tremendous competition both within the CCG market and with other
forms of entertainment. You discourage the newbie or the casual player who
feels like the game is only playable by the rich.

While I don't doubt the short term gains of gimmicks (including rarity ones,
which many companies have indulged in), it seems to me that the long term
business plan should be to broaden the player base - quantity over quality.
The real killing (that is, making a sustainable profit in the CCG industry)
comes with a large customer base. Some games can achieve this just by being
faddish (Pokemon) or being first (Magic), but most games have to work to hold
or build their popularity.

I play one game where R1s are necessary to be competitive. They've garnered
tremendous criticism. But, they haven't seemed to turn off a significant
portion of the player base ... yet. I have a feeling that they will contribute
to shortening the lifespan of the game. But, when the game dies, there will
likely be so many various reasons that you couldn't point to ultrarares as the
cause. So, companies will continue with the gimmicks, and worthwhile games
will continue to get underplayed.

Still, I know insiders who disagree. They believe that screwing the customer
does pay off and what really matters is having a good hook (often a great
license). I can somewhat forgive the view as nonWotC CCG companies do have to
worry about the short term.

Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
On Sat, 14 Jul 2001 19:36:02 GMT, "Jason Bell" <Jason...@mail.com>
wrote:

>"James Coupe" <ja...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote
>>, Ian Lee <cur...@aol.com> writes

>in the Deckmaster (TM, R, whatever) business, and they
>would just sell any card on demand by title (at booster
>price/booster size, or perhaps more, depending on demand
>for individual title), or at the very least in complete sets
>(at [set size/booster size]*booster price). Deckmaster is all
>about selling you cards that you don't need and don't want.

The above business model you describe results in one thing: A FAILED
BUSINESS. It will not generate enough profit to be self-supporting,
which is one very good reason that CCGs do not operate that way. CCG
companies cannot print-on-demand; they MUST make one huge print run
and then sell it. To support your business model would require either
that the company be able to predict accurately which cards would be in
high demand, or print FAR MORE cards than they could ever hope to
sell. Both expectations are unrealistic; the first is obvious, and
the second cuts into the profit margins sufficiently that you don't
make any money off it.

No sensible company will embark on any venture that is based on a
losing-profit model, unless (see "Microsoft") they make FAR more than
enough money from the rest of their business to be able to afford it.
See also "dot.bombs" such as Webvan.

>I agree that White Wolf is not Wizards, which is why I'm
>quite surprised that they won't sell sets. It's like a carnival

Because if you just sell a complete set, then collectors don't even
bother to buy the game, as a complete collection isn't ever worth
anything more than retail cost of the set? You know, CCG does stand
for "COLLECTIBLE" card game...? Not to mention that selling sets is
less than wonderful from the players' aspect; how many sets do you
want to buy in order to get 10 Disarms? And how many Weeks of
Nightmares will you get in the process... and how do you get rid of
the 5-7 you don't need?

Yes, the collectors do get the short end of the stick. But they do in
any form - look at Beanie Babies. Collectors buy something that has
no significant use, in hopes that it will be worth more to someone
else later than they originally paid for it. It's their gamble, and
they know it coming in. Nobody's getting fleeced THERE.

>game, but though I keep paying to play, at least I understand
>the implication of the carnie's refusal to let me just buy the
>stuffed animal.
>
>Of course we're being fleeced.

What a foolish statement. If we (the PLAYERS) were being fleeced,
then the 'best' cards would have filled up ALL the rare slots, instead
of the corner-case stuff like Week of Nightmares. Every single card
that the V:TES community has looked at and gone "oh, COOL!" (say,
Summon Soul) would have been rare, driving the value of cards up and
forcing people to buy huge numbers of boxes in order to be
competitive. Oh, and I can ASSURE you that the R1 cards would all
have been ultra-mega game-breaking powerful, too, to maximize the
demand from munchkins. The 11-cap Independents would have been vastly
more powerful than Inner Circle members, to make you chase after them
even more. No rares would have been in the pre-cons, and no reprints,
EVER, of any card that wasn't a common or vampire.

THAT's what being fleeced looks like. Instead, White Wolf is simply
attempting to make a decent profit, so that they can CONTINUE to make
a profit in the future. And it's pretty obvious, frankly, especially
when you compare Sabbat War and Final Nights to, say, a certain
Wizards game.

-- Derek

the argument away. If you argue that scarcity must be preserved

By the way, check out the current market price of the
M:tG collectors set, and you aren't even allowed to play

> Not to mention that selling sets is

Oh, oh, I know this one. Ten?

Hey, I know this one too. Ten?

Well, it's a Trading Card Game...

And what a bizarre point of view, especially when you consider how
many cards you'll need to buy to get anywhere near the neighborhood
of 10 Disarms. I say neighborhood since I'm allowing that you'll
be able to trade for some of them (though I've had little luck
on that particular card). Otherwise, you can still buy less than 10

>
> What a foolish statement. If we (the PLAYERS) were being fleeced,
> then the 'best' cards would have filled up ALL the rare slots, instead
> of the corner-case stuff like Week of Nightmares.

What a foolish statement. All that is required for the fleecing
is that many uncommon and rare cards be sought at an equal
or higher rate as the common or uncommon (respectively) cards.
This phenomenon is enough to cause those seeking
such cards to buy more of the incidental cards than they need or
want (for me, even the commons I use regularly choke my collection
box, such as Deflection and Wake). From another message in this
thread, you seem to agree, mentioning that you give many such cards
away (meaning you had to buy something you didn't need and didn't
want, and gave it away).

So, do you believe that a pick-pocket must steal every item on
your person to have robbed you? Must the carnival game be
totally impossible to win before it is considered unfair?
I think not.

> Every single card
> that the V:TES community has looked at and gone "oh, COOL!" (say,
> Summon Soul) would have been rare, driving the value of cards up and
> forcing people to buy huge numbers of boxes in order to be
> competitive. Oh, and I can ASSURE you that the R1 cards would all
> have been ultra-mega game-breaking powerful, too, to maximize the
> demand from munchkins. The 11-cap Independents would have been vastly
> more powerful than Inner Circle members, to make you chase after them
> even more. No rares would have been in the pre-cons, and no reprints,
> EVER, of any card that wasn't a common or vampire.

No, what you're describing is a (as you like to put it) "corner case"
example of fleecing, where WW would attempt to maximize the
number of packs the core competing community would have to buy
to get the required tournament cards. Even your example might
not maximize WW's profits, as it would turn off the casual
player who found that he could not play with the chaff he received
from a reasonable buy-in ($30 for most table-top games, but
you'd be hard pressed to put together a good deck from packs
at that level, maybe with the help of a starter, if you knew
going in what you wanted to play). Your situation above might
even turn off the serious but non-tournament player, who finds
that he can't get the cards he's read about without shelling out
a ridiculous (ok, more ridiculous) amount of money.
Your argument of "it could be worse" to counter the idea that
it is bad is sophomoric, particularly since I have already allowed
that it could be worse (WotC).

> THAT's what being fleeced looks like. Instead, White Wolf is simply
> attempting to make a decent profit, so that they can CONTINUE to make
> a profit in the future. And it's pretty obvious, frankly, especially
> when you compare Sabbat War and Final Nights to, say, a certain
> Wizards game.

Your position seems to rely on the presumption that since we could
be fleeced worse, we are not being fleeced. I provided my opinion
of that in the arguments above. I've already allowed that WotC is
worse, so I'm not sure what you're trying to argue in that vein.

If I have a chance to win the stuffed animal if I
play enough times, that doesn't make the carnival game
fair, regardless of whether the carnival's profits hinge
on my doing so.

- Jason Bell

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <c5c47.84389$ih.17...@typhoon.southeast.rr.com>, Jason
Bell <Jason...@mail.com> writes

>> The above business model you describe results in one thing: A FAILED
>> BUSINESS.
>
>Nope, plenty of gaming companies do quite well by including all
>the game pieces at once when the game is purchased.

So you're going to sell 90 of each card to every player in a "starter"?

What works for Monopoly, Clue, The Great Dalmuti or whatever isn't quite
the same as here, given the sheer diversity. Monopoly requires thirty
or so cards, a board and some distinct counters. You can even do the
money with pen and paper. This isn't true of a card game like Magic,
V:TES or whatever, unless you go for the trick of playing with
photocopies - which some people enjoy doing in friendly play in order to
try out a new deck idea.

>Some of these gaming companies produce game expansions, and
>include all the play pieces for the expansions as well.
>Oh dear, we don't have enough hotels, looks like we'll have to
>buy another Monopoly booster box. I think not.

You are constructing a very, very, very flimsy straw-man and
re-inforcing it with kindling.

>> It will not generate enough profit to be self-supporting,
>> which is one very good reason that CCGs do not operate that way. CCG
>> companies cannot print-on-demand; they MUST make one huge print run
>> and then sell it.

<Snip - technicalities of trading card game>

I think you'll find some elements of patent law got inserted here, too.
Whilst I understand the basics of British and European patent law,
American patent law is just plain screwy, from where I stand.

>As for your claim, it looks like a flat assertion from here,
>so I'll leave it alone.

Not true. The cost of printing a card game is, comparatively, huge. The
cost of paper/stock is high. (Remember, the cost of paper around the
world has gone up hugely over the last ten years.) The cost of printing
them is similarly high. The only reasonable way you can get this cost
down, for most companies, is to print in huge bulk, doing as much of the
print-run in one go as possible.

If you look around at the vast majority of card-games on the market,
you'll see this is pretty much true.

>> To support your business model would require either
>> that the company be able to predict accurately which cards would be in
>> high demand, or print FAR MORE cards than they could ever hope to
>> sell.
>
>This may be true for individual cards, but definitely not for sets.

Sets, being comprised of individual cards, inherit some of the truth
value. If you cannot predict, accurately, what it will require for
individual cards it makes it tricky, but not impossible, to predict for
a whole set.

>> No sensible company will embark on any venture that is based on a
>> losing-profit model, unless (see "Microsoft") they make FAR more than
>> enough money from the rest of their business to be able to afford it.
>> See also "dot.bombs" such as Webvan.
>
>Well, White Wolf embraced a bomb known as V:tES.

You have mis-understood the concept of something going titsup.com

dot.bombs are companies which inhale money with no business model. "Hey
guys, I'll put this up on the web.... and we'll make a penny a click
from advertising, never mind that it'll cost two cents a click to run.
It'll be cool and everyone will love it so of course they'll give us
lots of money!"

The production and sale of goods for a profit margin is a viable
business model. Jyhad has a proven track record in that even Sabbat
broke even, despite the best efforts of incompetence from Someone (tm)
at Wizards which fucked up the finance side. (Ryan S. Dancey confirmed
that Sabbat broke even. When it was pointed out that we had,
effectively, sold out two print runs, he was unable to satisfactorily
explain why a sell-out should result in breaking even only, IMHO.)

This is not a dot.bomb. This might be a somewhat risky proposition -
given that White Wolf have a "variable" track record with card games.
(Rage was fun, if broken, Changeling was Just Plain Bad (tm).) However,
it has a proven business model which can work. Risk can be minimised,
even if not eliminated, by doing many of the things White Wolf did. They
chose Sabbat for their first expansion because it was easiest to market,
thus providing a better guarantee of good sales. They produced a set
which carried many hard to obtain cards (those in Sabbat, primarily) due
to sell-outs of those sets. They got players involved at every level
e.g. LSJ as lead designer and rules authority, players local to White
Wolf to help them get up to speed with the game mechanics, talking to
people on newsgroups letting us know what was happening *in public*.
They created playable starters, thus making it easier to get players
into the game - "Hi, just buy this starter. It's not the best deck in
the world but you won't die horribly and you don't have to go out and
buy 5 starters and 76 boosters before you get enough cards to play a
Brujah deck."

A viable business model with minimised, even if not minimal, risk does
not equate to a dot bomb.

That this then led to a sell-out of the first print run of Sabbat War
suggests that something went well. That they went on from there to
produce a second print run, Final Nights and are still working on
Bloodlines suggests that something went well, especially given that
White Wolf are a company with a proven track record of sensibleness.

It has clearly been a very hot day. Your straw-man is starting to crisp
up.

>The number
>of bombs in Trading Card Games is probably as high or higher
>than dot.com flameouts, and with much smaller investments.
>Standard game production is a more successful profit model than
>the Trading Card industry, as far as I've seen. After all, Hasbro
>(standard game company) bought Wizards (most successful
>Trading Card company of all time).

The card game business model is a perfectly viable one - Magic has shown
us this, Pokémon has shown us this, leaving V:TES aside. However, you
have to a product that will sell. With Pokémon, this was created with
lots of mass media hype and such like so that the game would be popular
*regardless* of its playability. (Its mechanics are actually kinda
cute, in many ways, but a number of the special abilities are way, way
too random.) With Magic, there is also a highly clever, playable game
behind it demanding a lot of time, skill and effort. (As has been
pointed out before, its learning curve is different from many games -
you cannot just learn the basics and then everything slots in on top.)

There are many incompetent games companies out there, as there are many
incompetent companies full-stop, and it's all too possible to fuck up a
card game. But I can fuck up so many different products.

And when you look at the time Hasbro has been around, in its various
incarnations and acquisitions, and its aggressive business strategy in
that sense, it's quite a different kettle of fish to Wizards, maybe not
apples and oranges but perhaps acorns vs oak trees. It would also be
wise to reflect on just how many lines Hasbro has as compared to
Wizards.

It is also wise to reflect that, if Hasbro is incredibly successful in
the standard game market, it may not be worth a company's time competing
with them. The card game market neatly steps outside Hasbro's
traditional territory (prior to its acquisition of Wizards), thus giving
companies a whole different area to work with.

>> >I agree that White Wolf is not Wizards, which is why I'm
>> >quite surprised that they won't sell sets. It's like a carnival
>>
>> Because if you just sell a complete set, then collectors don't even
>> bother to buy the game, as a complete collection isn't ever worth
>> anything more than retail cost of the set? You know, CCG does stand
>> for "COLLECTIBLE" card game...?
>
>See above. If your argument is that sets cannot be sold because
>then the collectors will not be properly fleeced, you've given
>the argument away.

You are constructing a polar argument whereby someone gets a bargain or
gets fleeced, with no middle ground, or somesuch. It is your right to
use words like this, of course, but you must understand the difference
between how you use words and how other people understand them.

A person can pay a premium without being fleeced. A person can pay
below the going rate without getting a bargain. That's how the real
world works.

>If you argue that scarcity must be preserved
>to satisfy the secondary market, you've given the argument away.
>I'm mildly amused that you think this is even a debatable point.
>By the way, check out the current market price of the
>M:tG collectors set, and you aren't even allowed to play
>with those. That shows the falsity of your collectors won't
>bother to buy sets assertion.

*sigh*

He didn't say that collectors wouldn't bother to buy sets. If, however,
you could just go out and *buy* a set, straight off the shelf, what
value would it have to a collector? Significantly less than currently.

You also assume that a business model cannot cater for two distinct
facets. It is lucky for the rest of us that economics has gone somewhat
further than this. Careful manipulation of prices, rarity, power,
distribution and such like can produce a very smart business model which
appeals to both collectors and players, giving the players what they
need card wise whilst also providing tension in the market for
collectors.

>> And how many Weeks of Nightmares will you get in the process...
>
>Hey, I know this one too. Ten?

And how about if I want ten Wake with Evening's Freshness? Now, were I
to be buying starters, I could buy half a dozen of those, get all the
commons I really want and be left with a set of rarer cards I can trade
with or play with. Under your system, I'd have to buy TEN sets just to
get TEN WWeF. Jyhad's rarity system is somewhat more refined.

>> and how do you get rid of the 5-7 you don't need?
>
>Well, it's a Trading Card Game...

When you've just destroyed the rarity system, it's somewhat more
complex. Demand for trades and the ability to trade are somewhat
squashed when a person can just go out and buy a set.

>And what a bizarre point of view, especially when you consider how
>many cards you'll need to buy to get anywhere near the neighborhood
>of 10 Disarms.

You buy some cards, picking up, say, 2 Disarms. Then, using the
scarcity value of your rare cards as leverage, you trade with other
people.

It's not terribly difficult and is done by people playing V:TES all
round the world. Look at Legbiter's ToGP deck, Noal's Derange hoard,
Legbiter's Betrayer deck and such like.

>> What a foolish statement. If we (the PLAYERS) were being fleeced,
>> then the 'best' cards would have filled up ALL the rare slots, instead
>> of the corner-case stuff like Week of Nightmares.
>
>What a foolish statement. All that is required for the fleecing
>is that many uncommon and rare cards be sought at an equal
>or higher rate as the common or uncommon (respectively) cards.

And this just underlines where you significantly mis-understand
everything.

Does the fact that Pinot Noir is rarer than Random Cheap White Wine, and
more expensive, mean I'm being fleeced?

You are taking a company's business model, designed to make a profit so
that they can grow, expand, pay the wages, invest in research, spend
time creating products players want etc., and assuming that any element
of profit is "fleecing". After all, all that is required for fleecing
is that they charge us more than they could, surely? (An equally
unsupportable statement, compared to your own.)

>This phenomenon is enough to cause those seeking
>such cards to buy more of the incidental cards than they need or

Unfortunately for him, his definition isn't the actual one. James
used dictionary.com, and I'll use www.yourdictionary.com ...

Main Entry: fleece
Function: transitive verb
Date: 1537
Inflected Form(s): fleeced; fleec.ing
1. (a) to strip of money or property by fraud or extortion (b) to
charge excessively for goods or services

The applicable definition is (b).

So, for us to be getting fleeced, White Wolf needs to be charging us
excessively in some fashion for the "goods", aka the cards.

>"All that is required for the fleecing is that many uncommon and rare cards
>be sought at an equal or higher rate as the common or uncommon
>(respectively) cards. This phenomenon is enough to cause those seeking
>such cards to buy more of the incidental cards than they need or want (for
>me, even the commons I use regularly choke my collection box, such as
>Deflection and Wake). From another message in this thread, you seem to
>agree, mentioning that you give many such cards away (meaning you had to buy
>something you didn't need and didn't want, and gave it away)."

This "definition" is incoherent at best, and seems to revolve around
the assertion that fleecing is being "forced" to buy cards you don't
want in order to get cards you DO want. He then mentions two
Jyhad-original cards (which were printed under WotC's business model
and are therefore irrelevant to his own statement) to support this
assertion. And he then mentions something I said about how I ditch
some of my tons-of-commons and therefore I've been forced to buy
something I didn't need.

Since the base assertion is false, we can move on and determine
whether or not we're being charged excessively for our cards. How do
we do that? Well, you'd assume that if you were paying more for a
card than its actual value (plus a reasonable profit to the seller),
you were being charged excessively. Simple enough.

Cards, and V:TES itself, are a luxury item.

Main Entry: lux.u.ry
Function: noun
Date: 14th century
3. (a) something adding to pleasure or comfort but not absolutely
necessary (b) an indulgence in something that provides pleasure,
satisfaction, or ease

This means that nobody ever NEEDS V:TES cards. Being without your
cards does not mean you will either starve or sleep in the rain --
you're going to have to refuse to pay your rent to do that.

White Wolf is, currently, the only source of these cards. As such,
they set a price on them, and we choose whether or not to buy at that
price. They hold a monopoly on these goods; if we wish to have these
cards, we must buy from WW. This means that WW can set any price they
want to on these cards, and "random distribution" can be part of that
price.

But cards are a luxury. If we think their price is too expensive, we
don't buy the cards, we lose nothing, and WW loses money. This goes
right back to the basic unit of capitalism/economics that I've hit on
repeatedly in here:

A thing's value is what someone is willing to pay for it.

So as it turns out, if we're willing to pay their price, then we're
not being fleeced... because that's exactly what the value of the
cards is. For your $3.95[0], you're getting 7 common cards, 3
vampires, and 1 rare, in a random distribution, and you can decide
what piece of that $3.95 each card is worth yourself. Any subjective
value that people assign to the cards LATER is just that; a subjective
value that has absolutely no relation to the goods as they are sold.

When it comes right down to it, we're all busily fleecing each other.
Especially those singles-sellers who are selling individual copies of
R1s for $10-$15. THOSE people are fleecing you. But not White Wolf.
They only make that $3.95, and that's divided among 11 cards.

-- Derek

[0] I have no idea what an individual booster of FN costs, nor am I
even sure that 7/3/1 is the appropriate distribution of C/V/R inside
the booster. I don't care enough to look it up, and it isn't relevant
anyway, so please don't waste my time nit-picking.

To play Devil's Advocate here, you can make an argument that they (and anyone
else who uses rarity levels to the same effect) are fleecing their customers
by this definition. Consider how rarity levels inevitably make common cards
irrelevant after a certain number of packs have been purchased. (This would
not be true if common cards were typically used in decks at the same ratio to
rare cards that they appeared in packs. Even in Jyhad, however - without its
card limits and with some obvious attention being paid to which cards get used
more often, this is just not the case. The imbalance in frequency to utility
forces us to buy cards which are ultimately useless to us. Once you take this
into account, it's fair to say that after a point, you're paying the entire pack
price for only (the use of) the rare card and uncommon cards. Or only the rare
card in the extreme. The rest of the cards we're simply forced to accept to
complete the deal. Viewed that way, the cost of a pack for the single card or
the small handful of cards could be seen as excessive and that we're being
"fleeced".

Fred

Two incorrect assumptions; first, that you're being forced. It has
been shown time -and- again that it's possible to make competitive
decks of commons/uncommons only. You just don't get much variety that
way. Also, cards are a luxury; you never NEED to buy cards.

Second, that the cards are ultimately useless. I consider a pile of
"gift commons" to be highly useful insofar as encouraging new players
to keep playing; not to mention those commons are always available for
trade when you want to make, say, the 35-Cryptic-Mission deck. And if
you're into that sort of thing, there's always "rape the newbies"
where you offer them 10 of your spare commons for 1 of their rares.

>into account, it's fair to say that after a point, you're paying the entire pack

>the small handful of cards could be seen as excessive and that we're being
>"fleeced".

However, you DO get one rare card per pack. And theoretically, you
can trade that rare card to anyone else for a rare card that YOU want
more. In practice, this is probably not very difficult to manage at
all; it simply requires a very anti-materialistic attitude towards
one's own rares, and a significant determination to get one specific
rare (Noal's Derange hoard). You could also trade the vampires and
the commons in the same fashion.

Most people do not have such an attitude; they want somehow to get
either more rares than they've purchased, or they want to get other
rares without having to give up their own. If you want to have an
enormous variety of options, yes, you ARE going to have to buy a large
amount of cards, no matter what form they're sold in.

The price of the goods is still the same though, no matter what. The
perceived value afterwards is set by the PLAYERS, not by anything
White Wolf does. Any fleecing that's being done is all by the players
to themselves, or to other players.

-- Derek

pack. You will either undershoot (crappy rare or extra copies
of ones you don't want, a situation that becomes more likely
as the number of packs you buy increases) or overshoot (lucked
into a card you needed). My overarching point has been (or tried
to be) that a company with the interests of its players at heart
would tend to try to provide more and diverse methods to get
its product to its players. That's why it surpises me that WW
has not attempted such methods, the easist of which would be selling
sets. Of course WW has every right to do their business as they
see fit, I had just fancied them to be more customer-friendly
than the previous card company I patronized. I am prepared to
be wrong. You, of course, are allowed to counter with the idea
that to sell sets would crash the entire Deckmaster model,

Talk about someone with no sense of economics. Wow.

efficient economic decision. Compare that with the iterative pack
buying until success, or the transaction costs associated with
finding someone to trade for the cards (probably a bit
lower in places there are more players, depending on the card).

- Jason Bell

fleeced by someone else if not. You can continue to buy packs and be "fleeced"

the definition of being fleeced to something akin to getting robbed.

less than an optimal card collection, you can avoid being fleeced by this definition.
It's only those who choose to have the greater Jyhad CCG experience who must submit

invest money to get useful cards that start out at the steep rate (after all, they
already have enough commons!). So you haven't eliminated the problem, you've just
passed it along to another person.

commons like WwEF and Forced Awakening that will appear at lower levels but in
so many different decks that collections get strained to provide enough of them
to people who like to keep a lot of decks built simultaneously. But overall,
commons on average are not going to be 7 times as useful as rares.

It also requires skill and/or a lack of concern about getting the worst
of a trade. And you have to let go of ever wanting to play decks requiring
the things you give to get what you want. But yea, that's probably the
most efficient solution for people who need to economize on money. It
doesn't ultimately dispute what I'm saying, though.

Exactly.

The perceived value is always set by the customers. The act in question
would be called "bundling" in the high tech world. You have buy this to
get this. You have to buy 7 commons to get one rare. You don't need 7
more commons? Tough. That's the deal.

I'm not complaining about it myself. As you say, no one's holding a gun
to my head. And it's one of the ways, probably the major way, CCGs generate
sufficient sales and thus profit to insure the continued development of the
game. I'm just saying that forcing people to buy commons they don't need to
get rare cards they want is, IMHO, a decent enough reason to use the word
"fleece" WRT the practice given the dictionary definition you quoted.

Fred

That shows us how to print individual cards.

However, this involves:

1) No economies of scale - you are using the printer one by one,
sporadically, whenever
2) Man power for printing
3) Man power for mailing
4) Cost of shipping

If a card costs A under the current system, to print, under this system
it would be:

A + 1) + 2) + 3) + 4)

which is going to be significantly more. Labour is not cheap.

Hence my use of the term "competitive price". With this, singles are
going to cost as much as buying singles on the second-hand market does
now, or close thereto, I would've thought.

Let me fix that one: WW takes the card, prints it out on an
industrial-grade printing press (laser printers really just can't hack
it, even the really high-grade $30k stuff), and mails it to you?

Of course, industrial-grade presses aren't made to print things as
small as cards. That's why they do cards in sheets. =/

>If WW wanted to go a step beyond, the could contract with a printer,
>have the printer maintain the individual card templates, route all the
>purchases to the printer and have those card shipped directly from the

go through the roof. I'm sure that WW already subcontracts out to a
printing company as it is, because just the cost of maintaining that
kind of equipment is pretty damn high, and buying your own printer
just for a CCG means you have to figure out a way to make back the
cost of your printer, too...

convincing the printer to make TONS of itsy-bitsy print runs for
someone who wants 3 Disarms, 4 Relentless Pursuit, 2 Fire in the
Blood, and 4 Twisting the Knife (trick deck! =) one week, and ANOTHER
haphazard assortment the next...? I suspect the printing company
would laugh in your face. James already mentioned "economies of
scale", and there's a reason for it; it costs MONEY to set up and
prepare for just -one- print run, swapping out paper, etc. These guys
also have other customers, and it would take up so much of their time
printing for WW that it would be self-defeating to THEIR business.

The "print lots" model wasn't set up that way JUST to troll for
collectors and gamer-fish. =)

sets, or full sheets (2 of each C2) since that's probably easier.

I do understand that some find the collection and trading
of cards from random inputs to be an enjoyable pasttime itself.

But the current situation is the worst and most wasteful from
my point of view, where I would like the option to buy more cards
from current or past sets, but dare not, due to the implied
expense associated with buying pack after pack filled or nearly
filled with cards I cannot use. Artificial scarcity may very well
be the best way for WW and any Deckmaster producer to maximize
profits, but it's a lousy way to serve customers, in my opinion.

- Jason Bell

> lessened as described by other posters: more focused packs
> (clan specific packs) or less commons in packs (if card stock is
> a costly input, as WotC insisted the last time they raised pack
> prices that I remember). And it could also be lessened by any
> other method of reducing uncertainty (which is rarely a good
> thing in economic transactions), such as the pre-constructed
> decks that already exist, and my suggestion being selling
> sets, or full sheets (2 of each C2) since that's probably easier.

The "uncertainty" has its charms though. The manufacturer sells more
packs to folks like me who like to buy enough to hedge our bets. It
encourages game interaction in the form of trading. I don't care for
it but a lot of folks do. It's a deliberate disadvantage for the
customer so the manufacturer can sell more packs, some of it leading to
the waste you complain about. (As is/does the imbalance in commons to
rares that also inspires your dissatisfaction.) The brutal truth is
that CCG manufacturers do these things on purpose because they can and
because they have to to make the game profitable enough to be a viable
product. Customers accept these shenanigans because the problems presented
to them in the form of creating collections are fun (for many, at least)
to solve.

By the way, another thing the uncertainty does is make to make the
"limited" form of competition (sealed deck, draft, bubble leagues)
possible. Another aspect that's not on the top of my list. But lots
of folks really like that.

> But the current situation is the worst and most wasteful from
> my point of view, where I would like the option to buy more cards
> from current or past sets, but dare not, due to the implied
> expense associated with buying pack after pack filled or nearly
> filled with cards I cannot use. Artificial scarcity may very well
> be the best way for WW and any Deckmaster producer to maximize
> profits, but it's a lousy way to serve customers, in my opinion.

I've posted about this elsewhere. You need to think of this as part
of price of the product, just exactly like the printed price on the
pack of cards. White Wolf could do these things you suggest but might
well need to jack up the price per card several fold to make enough
money to keep the game going. The average person would rather have
the randomness and waste. (Much though the waste is regrettable in
terms of ecological considerations, IMO.)

Fred

Of course you mean that the marketing of sets is problemmatic
if they depress demand for boosters. If they do this, it would

and sold very well. But I take your point. Unfortunately,
the implication behind that point is not favorable to WW or
any Deckmaster R-U-C company, and very nearly concedes
the charge that random R-U-C is selling people cards that
they do not want and would not buy if given another option.

So, if the above situation is true and unavoidable, a solution
might be to market sets some time after the original release
of the expansion. That would lessen any expected dip in
booster demand, as demand would have fallen off by then
anyway, and actually pick up demand for that set's cards
overall. Can you think of any Jyhad or Vampire expansion
you would not buy at least one set of if offered at a price
anywhere in the neighborhood of booster price *
[set size/booster size]? Let's call it, for argument's sake,
$100 for a 400 card set, $50 for the smaller expansions.
Hmm, so maybe I wouldn't buy the original Jyhad at that
clip, or maybe just one, to have whatever cool packaging
would be involved. This would definitely stabilize the
secondary market (as cards known to be included in
pre-con decks have).

> Perhaps you have found your answer without even knowing it.
> If you buy the Pre-cons you are buying a set. You know what
> they contain and you can buy as many as you like at retail
> and receive cards that have a value over the price of the
> pre-con. If you want to own cards that exist outside of the
> pre-cons, then you gamble with buying a booster pack.

So there you go, WW already has its feet wet in set-selling,
so why not go further? Do they have marketing data
telling them that pre-con's have depressed overall card
sales? I doubt it, since the pre-con product is available for
at least 2 expansions now.

> Yes, but you must admit that the number of these ultra-rares has
> declined after they have added them to the pre-cons. Remember
> when a Taste of Vitae was nearly impossible to get.

Actually I don't, I have always had more than my share of
that one. But I do take your point. But try to take mine for
the cards that I want to play, but haven't been included
in pre-con "sets."

> <snip economist part. I live to fleece people.:)>
>
> > > This is another economic feature: the upward stickiness
> > > of prices.
> >
> > Until the game crashes again, of course.
> > I hope very much that WW does not attempt to model
> > their business on the frenetic set release that WotC
> > does for Magic (3 new sets per year or so), and I wonder
> > if the tournament people will ever destroy their player
> > base with Type I / Type II distinctions that turned Magic
> > into the hollow shell driven by adolescents spending
> > their parents' money. Time will tell.
>
> Hopefully that will never happen.

I strongly believe that it will happen, and such a crash
may be inherent in the R-U-C product model.
Artificial scarcity pushes up demand parallel with
additional players pushing up demand. When interest
in the game falls off, the additional player portion
of demand drops, pushing more cards into secondary
markets and driving prices for available product down,
depressing the scarcity portion, and the bubble burts.

This in itself may be a strong argument against selling
sets, since you're damaging your own scarcity engine,
but to use this argument against selling sets really
does give away the other argument that we're
being fleeced.

- Jason Bell

Jason Bell <Jason...@maildot.com> wrote a whole lot in this thread
paraphrased - "I think the game will crash again because the people in
charge are idiots that haven't learned from Magic's problems (tournament
scene), just its economic model."
He goes on to say:

> I strongly believe that it will happen, and such a crash
> may be inherent in the R-U-C product model.
> Artificial scarcity pushes up demand parallel with
> additional players pushing up demand.
> When interest in the game falls off, the additional player portion
> of demand drops, pushing more cards into secondary
> markets and driving prices for available product down,
> depressing the scarcity portion, and the bubble burts.

What secondary market?

There are three people selling singles on the net for VTES at this time.

Errol Trepanier (Immortal Grapple Cards
http://www.thelasombra.com/ImmortalGrappleCards.htm)
Bob & Joyce Trotter (Sengir Cards http://www.sengir.com)
Me (http://www.TheLasombra.com/cardtrader.htm)

Ebay is not a secondary market.

Ebay is the carnival desperate to fleece you.

Take a look at some of the higher priced "collectibles" some time. ie
Marianna Gilbert for $70 and up
Notice how one account keeps pushing the price higher and higher.
Notice how that account never wins an auction.
Its called bidding on your own auction and isn't supposed to happen,
but is a very common practice.

This is fleecing.

> This in itself may be a strong argument against selling
> sets, since you're damaging your own scarcity engine,
> but to use this argument against selling sets really
> does give away the other argument that we're
> being fleeced.

Illuminati: New World Order was one of the first 5-6 collectible card games
on the market.
The offered a Factory Set (included one of each card and some blank cards).

I will tell you that it killed booster sales completely in Seattle (where I
was at the time).

This was more a function of poor rules than a distribution argument, but
there
is no reason for someone who only collects the cards to buy anything other
than
a pre-packaged set. There are a huge number of those for this game.
Some because they can no longer find other players, some because they simply
like the card art.

Now, take any Deckmaster type of game.

You are promised a given number of rares, and specific number of uncommons,
and a specific number of commons.

This is exactly what you get when you buy either a booster or a starter.

If you are looking for something else, you need to utilize the "secondary"
card market.

The Trotters haven't had to buy any more Sabbat War or Final Nights since
their initial orders because there is NO DEMAND. There is, however, quite a
bit of foolishness going on with Ebay at any given time in any collectibles
category.

When sets are for sale on Ebay (and not by someone out to fleece you), they
have never come anywhere close to the price you mentioned, ie $100 for a
VTES set. The prices have been much closer to $60-70. I don't see how
producing a set and selling it for less than the price of a box of boosters
can ever help a company make money. Notice that the prices of the boosters
are set (and raised) by the price of paper, not by the popularity of the
game (in general).

Please redifine your use of the term "secondary" market, and describe how
the presence of one is anything but good for the game.

Carpe noctem.

Lasombra

http://www.TheLasombra.com

I did not mean to imply all that is paraphrased above.

I did not mean to claim people at WW were idiots, I was
merely continuing a thread discussing possible reasons in
favor and against various ways to merchandise Vampire cards.

For all I know, WW may be a clan of evil geniuses desperate
to claw all my money away from me by printing a great game
but making the pieces difficult to obtain, or they may be
corporate geniuses who infallably know bad things will happen
if they deviate from standard product distribution schemes.

I think all these possibilities are relatively independent
of whether the game will eventually crash, but they may
affect the timing. It seems to me obvious that you
cannot keep printing cards forever expecting people
to keep buying them, especially when the marketing
involves imposing scarcity, unless you continue to
produce more and more powerful cards, at which time
another problem arises, which destroys the game from
the other side.

I'm told there is a great deal of selling on E-Bay, and I understand
that there is a newsgroup dedicated to the selling of these cards
(haven't subscribed). Smaller markets for singles can be found
at various retail outlets that carry V:tES product.

My definition of the secondary market is everyone who sells cards
outside of the packaging. That's right, if you sell a card to your
roommate for a dollar, you're part of the secondary market, though
if you trade him for another card, I suppose you are not, for this
definition.
The primary market is the sales in the product as sold by WW:
Packs, starters, and boxes of both, at retail price or at discounts
from distributors.

> Ebay is not a secondary market.
>
> Ebay is the carnival desperate to fleece you.

that market, but nonetheless.

> Marianna Gilbert for $70 and up
> Notice how one account keeps pushing the price higher and higher.

You may be right, but this phenomenon itself is a function of
how E-Bay takes bids. If I really want an item at auction, I
give E-Bay a very high reserve price, and if my reserve
price is eventually above the winning price, my name will always
be the name with the high bid, even as other bidders push
the price up closer to my reserve price.

> Notice how that account never wins an auction.

If both these things are true, then I just don't know
what's going on there, and you may be right.

> Its called bidding on your own auction and isn't supposed to happen,
> but is a very common practice.
>
> This is fleecing.

Maybe, but it's also called garden variety fraud.
It's also very difficult to bid up your own auction
without accidentally winning it, and thereby being
unable to sell the card to someone who bid an acceptable
amount, plus owing E-Bay the fee associated with the
sale to yourself. Or maybe I'm missing something
important about what happens then the winning bidder
"backs out" of a sale.

games

cards).

I
> was at the time).

were in the area of degeneracy and game balance. Plus, there
was another way to play Illuminati, which is a ton of fun and
much better conceived than the TCG. By the way, how were
booster sales of INWO at the time, and do you think the set
offering increased total sales or not?

> there
> is no reason for someone who only collects the cards to buy anything other
> than

discuss (between all-out flames directed at me for having the
temerity to criticize WW and the random packaging model of card
sales) involves delaying set availability until the boosters have been
on the market for some period of time. So for the argument, I'm
accepting the hypothesis that set offerings depress the sales of
other product (which seems a bit of a no-brainer, since a portion
of total demand must be split by the new product. I imagine the
pre-con decks do the same thing, I know they reduced the number
of boosters I bought, though probably did not reduce my total
purchase), and envisioning a double bump in the sales curve for a set's
sales overall, one for the initial release, and another when sets are
available.

>
> You are promised a given number of rares, and specific number of
uncommons,
> and a specific number of commons.
>
> This is exactly what you get when you buy either a booster or a starter.

Excepting the occasional mis-sort (we all remember the odd Jyhad starter
with rares as far as the eye could see). By the way, I don't believe any
Deckmaster pack has ever guaranteed the rarity sorting of its contents

a

collectibles
> category.

Well, then I'd better get over there, as there are quite a few Sabbat War
and Final Nights cards I really want, but am not willing to wade through
tons of the cards I already have plenty of. But think how exciting it would
be if I could patronize WW directly for the demand I have for their
merchandise.

> When sets are for sale on Ebay (and not by someone out to fleece you),
they
> have never come anywhere close to the price you mentioned, ie $100 for a
> VTES set. The prices have been much closer to $60-70. I don't see how
> producing a set and selling it for less than the price of a box of
boosters
> can ever help a company make money. Notice that the prices of the
boosters
> are set (and raised) by the price of paper, not by the popularity of the
> game (in general).

I wasn't trying to produce an exact price point, I was merely putting forth
a back-of-the-napkin number for discussion purposes, and I hoped to err
on the high side to avoid a certain kind of criticism. But make your point
plain, do you beleive that sets would not sell, or that the selling would
depress the booster market? I can't imagine how it could be both.

> Please redifine your use of the term "secondary" market, and describe how
> the presence of one is anything but good for the game.

I never claimed otherwise, and I believe that the secondary market
is vital for filling demand that the card producers seem unwilling
to do. My only claim vis-a-vis the secondary market is that set selling
would stabilize the market prices for singles, which is a good thing.
I assume you must agree, considering your blasts of E-Bay auctions.

it can generate more wealth. The only other thing you can do with
RDI, besides SPEND it (wastefully if possible) or INVEST it (turning
it into non-disposable income), is STUFF IT IN YOUR MATTRESS AND SLEEP
ON IT. And if you DO put it in your mattress, you're a damned moron
for a number of different reasons.

So let's see... we're being fleeced out of money that we were going to
waste on something ANYWAY? I'm sorry, no. Toss aside all the
dictionary definitions, toss aside all the random assorted semantic
bullshit that has flown back and forth; if you were going to blow the
money ANYWAY, it doesn't MATTER what you blow it on. Nobody held a
gun to your head and said "Buy V:TES!" The only thing that matters is
if after spending the money, you enjoyed the result. That's what
disposable income is, man, it's there to be DISPOSED OF. And if you
bought cards and DIDN'T enjoy the result, I'm sorry, and I hope you
have better luck with your next waste of money. But frankly, every
last one of you DID enjoy your cards to some degree or other. Some of
you probably froliced with them, inhaling the new-card smell... some
of you were more subdued, i'm sure. But yes, ALL of you enjoyed the
purchase. All of you. Or you wouldn't be here on this group, and you
wouldn't GIVE a shit about V:TES.

Have any of us been fleeced? NO. Entertainment cannot be measured in
a pint jar, nor can a price be set on it. This is why front-row
concert tickets sell for hideously expensive amounts of money now;
because people get sufficient entertainment out of it to make it worth
their time to BUY the damn things in the first place, and because
despite the expensive price, the concerts STILL SELL OUT. Are we
being fleeced for concert tickets by Ticketmaster? NO. If we REALLY
objected to Ticketmaster's prices, we just wouldn't GO, because it's;
guess what, DISPOSABLE INCOME. We would simply dispose of it
somewhere else that gave us more entertainment at what we thought was
a reasonable price.

That's all there is to it. You can fling numbers around, and you can
debate the meanings of the words until the cows come home, and even
until the cows wake up with hangovers the next morning... but it's
just plain not possible to be ripped off on something that's a total
waste of money anyway. And yes... it IS a total waste of money. It's
one of the more fun wastes I can put my finger on, but it is a TOTAL
waste of money.

The only people fleecing us are we ourselves. We choose to buy the
product. We open up our OWN wallets and purses, without having our
arms twisted behind us, and lay out money for cards. We know exactly
what we're getting into when we buy the product, and we SOLD OUT two
sets of Sabbat War. Clearly we are not dissatisfied; and clearly we
are not being fleeced.

Enough said, already. If you're that pissed at White Wolf because
they won't sell you a set, please fuck off and go play Doomtown --
because unless I'm mistaken, its makers WILL sell you a set right now.
Of course, there's a catch to it.

-- Derek

On Wed, 18 Jul 2001 04:57:06 GMT, Jason Bell wrote:

>It seems to me obvious that you
>cannot keep printing cards forever expecting people
>to keep buying them, especially when the marketing
>involves imposing scarcity, unless you continue to
>produce more and more powerful cards, at which time
>another problem arises, which destroys the game from
>the other side.

Th usual model is to rotate cards out of play in some manner. Magic
has explicit set rotation. L5R has its storyline formats. Decipher
starts against with a fresh game on the same subject (Stars Wars,
Young Jedi, Jedi Knights).

Vampire hasn't yet reached this point but here's an interesting
snippet from Dave Wiiliams, the AEG designer, apropos L5R Gold edition
(which has changed that game's card backs at the behest of the US
Olympic committee).

>Excuse me, but I quit playing Vampire when I was told that I couldn't
>use my Jyhad cards in tournaments any more. That may have changed
>since then, but you can't tell me that it didn't happen.

Doomtown is now being terminated by AEG. One interesting detail was
the format of their last set. This was produced as a fixed set of
~200 cards in a useful card box for $50. What's interesting is that
I'm fairly sure that they did it this way to cut costs - no sorting,
no collation, no starters, no booster wrappers. They expected it to
sell mainly to the afficionados. I certainly liked it and now have 11
sets.

If you don't like being fleeced then put your money where your mouth
is and buy CCGs only in fixed format - fixed starters for Final
Nights, fixed starters for Firestorm, the fixed sets and starters for
Doomtown, the One With Everything set for INWO, etc. Of course,
you'll miss out out on all those VTES rares but you don't need them,
right?

Andrew

Marijava Ghoul, which was printed 1 time on the unccommon sheet and 2 times

correctly a "U2" - in 74% of the packs. In 26% of the packs, you'd have to
settle for two of the "U5"s.

Anyway, all the Sabbat packs, as far as I know, had two rares.

I disagree with this statement. Ebay has definately become a part of the
secondary market. In fact for some "collectables" it has almost taken over
setting secondary pricing from printed price guides. This is the case in my
other hobby, model railroads. Stores that used to sell used trains really
cheap have over the last 3 years begain to charge almost exactly what those
items tend to go for on ebay. At train shows you frequently hear, "That's
not even what I could get for it on ebay". Like it or not ebay is rapidly
becoming the secondary market for most collectables. You don't see this as
much with V:tes yet because the market is still so small. There is not
really enough people selling V:tes on ebay to get good averages for a
certain box, card, etc.. If V:tes continues to grow it will eventually
happen...

>Ebay is the carnival desperate to fleece you.

No, ebay is an auction. In most cases people pay what they are willing to
pay.

>Take a look at some of the higher priced "collectibles" some time. ie
>Marianna Gilbert for $70 and up
>Notice how one account keeps pushing the price higher and higher.
>Notice how that account never wins an auction.
>Its called bidding on your own auction and isn't supposed to happen,
>but is a very common practice.

True this happens. However it takes someone who is willing to pay such
insane amounts to drive the price up. A shill can't drive the price up
without someone else to bid against. If he bids against him self he is a
dope because he gets stuck paying all the ebay fees. This practice is also
not allowed and ebay is taking steps to track down such people and
permanently remove all their user id's. It is also very easy to check out
such dishonest behavior by checking bidding records.

Most often the insane prices on ebay are not the result of shill bidding. In
my experience there are 3 basic reasons auctions get bid up to crazy prices:

1) Lack of knowledge. Often people will bid on something they want without
having any idea (or simply not caring) what the items value really is. They
see it, they want it, they are going to get it. It's that simple. Such
people will pay $10 for $1 Hot Wheel just because they want it.

2) They can't get it were they live. I have frequently sold model railroad
equipment to people in Australia, Europe, and even Japan. Once you add
shipping cost they often pay much more then I could find the item for around
here. Why do they pay that much? They simply can't find the item were they
live. It's worth it to them just to get the item.

3) They want the item NOW. Instant gratification. They don't want to wait
until the item is in less demand, more available, or on sale. They have to
have it right now. Some people will pay insane amounts of money to get what
they want as soon as possible. Remember the fools paying and extra $20,000
just to be one of the first to get a Viper...

In short I believe ebay eventually does set secondary market price. If a
bunch of people are willing to pay $20 for Ezmerelda, and that card sells
for an average of that price on ebay for 6 months or so, that will be what
the secondary price starts to become. You will have some crazy stuff from
shills and nuts, but eventually that will dissipate and real price will
start to become clear and set.

february) and Z is the letter roughly corresponding to the number of weeks
into the month (that is, if the message is dated from the first of the month
to the sixth of the month, the letter is 'A'. 'B' for 7th-13th, 'C' for

It doesn't work that way. Certain commons and uncommons will always be
in demand and sellable but the vast majority of them are not. In fact,
few singles dealers even bother to sell such cards. Those that do will
quote something like a quarter a card or something that represents their
price for bothering to go find one. And under no circumstances are these
people selling all the commons (and likely not even the uncommons) they
open. If they could, then there'd be some trade value to the ones I pull
out of packs. Which there isn't.

So all you're doing is just what I said in my last post. You're paying
a singles dealer to do all the same dirty work I'd have to do - buy packs,
throw away the untradable stuff I can't use, and go find someone to trade
the stuff I need to me for the stuff I've got too much of. Yes, that answers
the immediate issues Jason Bell was complaining about. But it answers them
in a kind of obvious way by throwing money at the problem until it goes
away. It's like bitching about such-and-such a car company builds shoddy
cards which keep breaking down and having someone suggest taking the car to
an auto mechanic. It's not the point.

> Yes, buying all your cards from a secondary dealer will cost more per
> card than buying boosters. But like I said, the alternate delivery
> systems (cards on demand) others have proposed would also drive up the
> cost per card. Selling sets wouldn't necessarily raise the cost per
> card, but that model still results in customers buying cards you don't
> want: two Clan Loyalties per Dreams of the Sphinx in every Giovanni
> Starter, for example.

Yea, I understand. Mind you, I'm not necessarily a proponent of having
White Wolf sell sets or singles or any other particular way of doing it.
But I see Jason's point. Instead of having singles sellers get a cut and
still having to deal with a bunch of wasted cardboard, why not let people
order just exactly the cards they want to have in their collection. It
might cost more per card but in theory it would be more efficient - at
least from a materials standpoint.

My fear, and probably a lot of other people here are trying to express the
same thing, is that from a labor standpoint, this is likely to *not* be the
most efficient way to print and sell cards for a constructed card game.
To lower the cost, cards need to be printed in huge print runs. This involves
predicting how many of what cards will be ordered. And having individuals go
pick out, pack, and ship singles is not likely to nearly be as efficient as
prebuilt, prepackaged groups of cards, whether randomly ordered or in specific
grouping such as the precon decks. And the trouble with precons or whole card
sets or any form of planned sets is that they may not be the groups anyone
wants (as you say, "two Clan Loyalties per Dreams of the Sphinx in every
Giovanni Starter).

So ultimately, I question if the business can be improved substantially in any
way. It would be interesting to have someone try this and see if they can make
it work somehow.

Fred

[ramble]
I completely agree (with Steve). Further, I'd say that the online
auctions (of which Ebay is a particular one) are a key part of the
secondary market, and are in perfect position to set secondary prices,
because:
(a) They have global scope.
(b) They're real-time.
(c) They track actual sales transactions, as opposed to reported
transactions or averages.

So what does that mean? It means that the highest bidder will be
drawn from interested parties from various markets across the world,
each with their own local price structures that may be higher or lower
than each other. Since the highest bidder wins, the closed
(successful) auctions represent the high-end of the distribution of
all bidders' highest bids for an item, usually from bidders that live
in the "high-price" market area, or other bidders that compete with
them.

It does seem then, that local/regional supply shortages or demand
spikes can provoke price action on the (global) auction sites. It is
very much up to the market participants to compare the local trend to
the auction site, and alter their participation as necessary.

And since everybody can see the results (often over time), prospective
buyers and sellers can refer to the up-to-date transaction record, and
the in-progress auctions, to evaluate their own price positions. If
the difference is significant (as measured by the individual), their
acceptable buying or selling price will change, generally depending on
how much a participant's cost model is tied to qualities like pride,
inventory costs, impulsiveness, disposable income, purpose for item,
etc.

As an illustrative (and recent) exercise, compare any vendor list to
the comparable card prices on an auction site, and note the
differences, particularly between the list and the most 'expensive'
site. The resulting difference represents either unclaimed or
unwanted money.

The big deal about CCGs, particularly CCG singles, is that sales don't
exist outside of the secondary market. We can't call up White Wolf to
order singles (although if they can print up a few dozen more Blood
Tears, I'll buy them ;).

[/ramble]

Yes, I read the post, but I strongly disagree with the
sentiment. I think it is wrong-headed to insist on the
"put up with it or get out, nobody's forcing you" position,
in the same way I disagree with the "that's the way it is
in America, if you don't like it leave." I believe something
more along the lines of Carl Schurz:

"Our country, right or wrong. When right, to be kept right;
when wrong, to be put right."
- Address, Anti-Imperialistic Conference, Chicago, 10/17/1899

So I see nothing wrong in having a discussion on how the
problems I see with TCG's in general and V:tES in
particular might or might not be solved, regardless
of whether those problems are currently enough to
drive me away from the game.

But more to the point, if I want to play with
additional game pieces for this game, and I
want to buy those pieces from the game's
manufacturer, I am indeed forced to buy
cards I don't need in addition to the ones
I actually want, with no certainty of actually
getting the ones I want. This is a very peculiar
feature in an economic transaction,
and the only similar arrangement I can
think of is those prize machines that they
set up next to the gumball machines.

- Jason Bell

Messages.Author: Noal McDonald
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott <fre...@netcom.com> wrote

> The implication you seem to be making is that constructable card
> games *must* be sold this way.

VTES is not just a "constructable" card game. It is a _collectible_
card game and a _trading_ card game. As such, absolutely it must be
sold that way. To do otherwise would be ludicrous.

Selling a set of cards in such a a manner as to make them equally
accessible reduces their value in the secondary market to nil and thus
destroys the marketability of the contents of that set to collectors.

Notice that this is much different than Lunch Money. When was the last
time that you saw individual Lunch Money cards being auctioned on
e-bay?

> It is not necessary the that the concepts of constructable/deckbuilding games

> and tradable/randomly assorted cards in pack be joined at the hip.

True. But selling a card set as a complete set and selling it a
collectible set _are_ mutually exclusive. To believe otherwise is to
demonstrate complete naivete regarding the economics of the secondary
market and how it affects the profitibility of CCGs.

The only reason one would issue collectible cards as a set is because
the cards are no longer in print, there is sufficient demand for them
and the company no longer has interest in marketing *those* cards as
collectible. That is not to say that future expansions on that set
cannot be marketed as collectible.

Regards,
Noal

In message <68f2e9f8.01072...@posting.google.com>, legbiter
<legb...@my-deja.com> writes

>Since the mechanics of Aeon are fairly classic storyteller stuff [ie
>the same framework as VtM] it should be easy to map vampires onto the
>Trinity: Battleground system.

(Moving into RPG weirdness.)

This isn't quite true (though it might as well be, maybe). (Not
including some of the changes between 2nd and 3rd re: botches.) The
whole dots things still exists, but a lot of the dice-rolling rules are
quite different. The dot thing is probably most important for mapping,
but the rules are quite interestingly changed.

e.g. VtM a variable target number (difficult) for the dice, below which
is a fail, else it's a success. Then count the successes. Aeon changes
this to a system whereby the target number is fixed, but the number of
successes you need to get is varied.

VtM generally requires the Storyteller to make arbitrary decisions a lot
of the time about traits. (e.g. "Hmmm.... you're going to have to sing
for a long time and be damn good at it to shatter all these glasses.
Roll Stamina + Performance.") Whilst you *can* do this Aeon, it prefers
to default to tying them all in to the most useful ones. The subtle
changes, where a Storyteller might think "Hmmm.... Let's have Charisma +
Leadership instead of Manipulation + Leadership" are less likely to
occur if you have a mind-set of "This normally goes with this, I need to
justify my deviation."

It's mostly just fiddling round the edges, but it makes things a bit
more tricky when you start trying to cross the two over.

But then, crossing things over in White Wolf games always was kinda
kooky. (This has a difficult of the target's Humanity. Hmm.... He's a
Changeling. Erm?)

Messages.Author: Lemar Johnson
Messages.Body:
A major digression...

Andrew S. Davidson <a...@csi.com> wrote in message news:
<CCG that have tried other player-friendly pack-outs -
> Xxxenophile, INWO, Rolling Thunder - have all flopped. Just be glad
> that the game doesn't have ultra-rares too.
>
> Andrew

I know this is an old(er) post, but I felt the need to point out what
someone had mentioned earlier -- TCGs fail for a variety of reasons.

I am very familiar with L5R and INWO. Rolling Thunder (a format AEG
was using for L5R and a few other games) was indeed over-easy to
collect for collectors, but what really hurt it was the horrible way
it was distributed. (The Powers That Be had a lengthy post about it --
none of the distributors understood how it was going to work.)

A more clear example of secondary issues hurting a game is with INWO.
The Factory Set -- the complete basic set -- stimulated game sales.
Collectors *still* bought cards, while players shelled out for the
whole deal. Trick is, you need duplicates to play INWO, lots of them
(sound familiar?), so players bought boosters, too. I can't make even
a portion of my most capable or fun decks with my two factory sets.
Throw in the boosters and it all works. (INWO would do fine to have
only two rarities -- common and rare -- and the synergy of the Factory
set with random cards supports this assertion. The Factory Sets really
only provide the hard-to-get, generally unique cards.)

What killed INWO was horrible support from SJG. Its first expansion
was bantam in scope. It didn't have the flavor that many people were
expecting -- it didn't look enough like a conspiracy game. The second
expansion killed the game dead. Many people love that the SubGenius
expansion was a boxed set -- but they didn't give a damn about
SubGenius. It would be equivalent to making a VtES expansion about
fast food.

Sounds amusing, but it would not be a good thing.

Combine this with poor support on other fronts (which I won't get
into) and we have our culprit: Steve Jackson killed INWO -- killed it
but good, he did.

Boxed sets work, and they don't hurt collectability as long as the
card faces are CLEARLY different from the randomly sorted packs. INWO
was never that popular, admittedly, but until after Assassins (the
first expansion) its sales were continually increasing. Note that the
Factory Set cards were completely different in color than the
randomized ones, making them visually distinct -- this is essential.
People were still, obsessively, attempting to collect a set or two of
a game not many people played and completely ignored the Factory set.
I have no data on whether or not the Factory Set influenced the
singles market, unfortunately. Anecdotally, I can say that INWO
players I was aware of bought singles to increase the number of
duplicates in decks (to avoid having to buy a Factory Set for just two
cards -- the inverse of why we buy singles for games without such
sets) or to complete sets in the first place. That is not empirical
evidence, only experience.

Still (to go beyond speaking of INWO or Rolling Thunder), I have seen
no examples of the reprint of a card in any game -- especially when
the reprint is in a different format (color or art changes, for
example) -- having a detrimental effect on the singles market, even
less the set sales itself. The value of the original card for
collectors was in its rarity, not its playability.

Similarly, foils of rares that take up rare slots encourage collectors
without hurting players. This holds for my experience, and for the
games I play.

You may now return to your scheduled haughty and snappish postings.
:-)

-- Lemar Johnson

(2) If a straight line fit is required, obtain only two data.

The collectability of VtES is a secondary byproduct of its having many
components that are individually sold. No WoTC TCG is marketed as a
CCG. Selling a set of game components that are independent of the
components that collectors are buying is not ludicrous, especialy if
the sets are clearly in a different format than the non-set
components. As a matter of fact, it generates sales as the manufacurer
can now sell such components in bulk, defraying costs.

> Selling a set of cards in such a a manner as to make them equally
> accessible reduces their value in the secondary market to nil and thus
> destroys the marketability of the contents of that set to collectors.

Do explain Heroes of Rokugan, a very, very small set of cards sold in
L5R. Singles from HoR sale ludicrously well. Many players found the
set utterly abhorrent because of the price. Collectors -- *collectors*
-- often broke the rules and created false accounts to buy more sets
than they were technically allowed. The cost of HoR was around $80 --
for about 20 cards. WotC limited its own profit on the set by limiting
the print run and accessibility to the set; it would have successfuly
sold the set if it had printed the set several times over.

This is not a happy example of what sets do to a game, IMHO, but it is
an example of sets making lots of money for the parent company without
killing the game.

> Notice that this is much different than Lunch Money. When was the last
> time that you saw individual Lunch Money cards being auctioned on
> e-bay?

Lunch Money has no components which can add to or modify the game.
There is no reason to sell individual cards in Lunch Money because
additional copies of cards in Lunch Money do not add to the enjoyment
of the game. In fact, they hurt the game. (Twenty extra copies of
Humuliation is funny for the first minute, then it gets stupid, fast.)
With a TCG, multiple copies of cards can and do add to variability
and, thus, enjoyment of the game, moreso if the game in question does
not have card limits.

> > It is not necessary the that the concepts of constructable/deckbuilding games
> > and tradable/randomly assorted cards in pack be joined at the hip.
>
> True. But selling a card set as a complete set and selling it a
> collectible set _are_ mutually exclusive.

This statement is completely false. If the components differ, even
slightly, in a set and in the random assortment, then the two products
are different. If your assertion was true, foiled versions of cards
would be considered exactly the same as normal cards they represent by
collectors. In addition, as we have already mentioned, VtES is not
marketed as presenting a collectable set.

>To believe otherwise is to
> demonstrate complete naivete regarding the economics of the secondary
> market and how it affects the profitibility of CCGs.

To make blanket statements like the above is not a little arrogant and
very off-putting. :-)

(It might be best if we comment upon arguments and statements made and
not make accusations, like the implied insults within the previous
poster's and my own comment above. Of course, I'm guilty of it even as
I disparage it, but I'm pretty sure I'm an immature jerk which puts it
in-character.)

> The only reason one would issue collectible cards as a set is because
> the cards are no longer in print, there is sufficient demand for them
> and the company no longer has interest in marketing *those* cards as
> collectible. That is not to say that future expansions on that set
> cannot be marketed as collectible.

Um, again, VtES isn't marked as collectable, ever. And, again,
reprints have never hurt the collectability of a previous set as,
well, collectors can read and they will consider the reprints to be
separate entities, distinct from previous sets. I understand that they
call such reprints, um, reprints. If reprints are a part of a new set,
collectors buy the new set and the reprints as part of that set
(without those reprints, the new set is not complete). Players have
increased access to old cards at the expense of not having a brand,
new card where the old one would be -- a price that players are
willing to pay, depending upon the play-quality of the old card.
Neither side is hurt if this is handled well.

-- Lemar Johnson

completely. I tend to take the angle that it wasn't in WOTC's best
interest to actually grow their licensced CCG work. The scenario
seems clear: Firm A is first entrant into the widget production, and
gains superior market position. It then acts as an outsourcer to
design and produce widgets for other firms B,C, and D.

as a piece to the above scenario.
