No need. Just have posters like Coupe declare me an idiot, a troll,
and ignorant of economics (a claim more hilarious to me than I'll
ever tell him).

> There is
> no particular reason that VTES *must* be a "collectible" card game nor a
> "trading" card game - other than the fact that it was started that way
> and to change it now would be a ripoff to people who paid what they paid
> for their various cards under that understanding. If that's not what you
> meant then to simply do it otherwise from the start does not strike me as
> ludicrous.

There is even less particular reason since the CCG industry has already
shifted to a TCG industry with little difficulty once confronted with
its own desires to re-print cards for its own profit, and shifted yet again
to a known-quantity card game industry with pre-con decks (ever
since M:tG's pre-con's for Tempest, if I recall correctly). Even
early M:tG dabbled with sets, though not in tourney-legal format
(though V:tES will likely never even try that, as most casual players
will accept any new distinctive card backs as just another in a long
line of card-back changes).

> > Selling a set of cards in such a a manner as to make them equally
> > accessible reduces their value in the secondary market to nil and thus
> > destroys the marketability of the contents of that set to collectors.
>
> Assuming we're discussing how it would have worked to start it out that
> way and not convert now, I don't see your problem. You're right. Selling
> a set of card in such a manner as to make them equally accessible reduces
> their value in the secondary market, not to nil but in terms of the usual
> discount for used game components. But still, that would certainly reduce
> the marketability of the contents of that set to collectors, as you say.

Not neccessarily. Selling sets merely stabilizes secondary markets for
any card. If the sets are in-print, the maximum value of any card or
any group of cards is easily determined (as it is currently with Dreams
of the Sphinx), while individual cards within that set can stil vary,
though with an inihibited range (limited by the current desirability
of other cards in the set and total set price).

Setting all that aside, I distinctly remember Tom Wylie loudly complaining
that what Noal claims to be vital was never a goal nor in any way an
intended consequence of the Deckmaster card distribution formula
(This was way back during M:tG's painful transitioning from a CCG to a
TCG, during an online discussion of reprints)

> > > It is not necessary the that the concepts of
constructable/deckbuilding games
> > > and tradable/randomly assorted cards in pack be joined at the hip.
> >
> > True. But selling a card set as a complete set and selling it a
> > collectible set _are_ mutually exclusive.
>
> Oh, absolutely.

Maybe, but there are no CCG's, so this is a moot point.
Even if it were a CCG, as long as the print run were
limited (even in very large instances of limited), the
set is still in some sense collectible. But even so...

Since we're talking TCG's, the fact that game pieces
can be used in ways other than fixed proportions, some
game pieces have more functionality (at least to some
players), so while sets can ease the work of consumers
who merely want to collect one of each card, they maintain
tradability for those who want more copies of certain
cards than other cards, so the tradability of the game
is maintained.

So what you're left with is the argument that
sets should not be sold because it would prevent
pure collectors from buying a bunch of cards they don't
want (and I suppose deny them the enjoyment of spending
massive resources in the joy of discovering if their Nth pack
has provided the card or cards they need to finish their task),
that selling them would harm the secondary market (for which
WW earns not one penny), or that offering them would
bankrupt WW and destroy V:tES through some
mechanism that exists as an article of faith.

- Jason Bell

If anyone cares, here is the original letter.....
-~-~-~-~-~-~-~-~-~-
Friends:

Hi, this is Mavra, aka Peter, the janitor at Wizards of the Coast.
Several of
you have written me with your concerns on the name change of our game
Jyhad to
V:TES, and the subsequent removal of the word Jyhad from the contents of
the
game. This letter is a response to those letters, and the letters I
haven't
yet received.

This was a tough decision as you can probably imagine. And in truth, I
think
it was one of those times we as a company genuinely faced a no-win
scenario.

Making the change seriously risks killing the game and pissing off our
customer base. We have never suffered from the delusion that this would
somehow help the sales or popularity of the game.

Keeping it the way it is, I believe, is immoral. It's as simple as
that. I
can't have a game like this in my catalog and look my Israeli
distributor
straight in the eye.

I know a lot of you don't feel that there's anything immoral about using
the
word Jyhad in a game. But our products are reaching new customers and
countries that never cared about traditional roleplaying games and such,
and
may of them disagree. Of course I didn't see this as a problem
originally,
but I have a middle-class WASP background and spent many years thinking
the
United States was the center of the universe and that the thoughts of
people
in the Middle East didn't really matter. Fortunately I met Beverly and
she
taught me how much of an ass hole I was for thinking that way, and so at
the
age of twenty-eight I grew up and got a life.

Folks, we just can't pull this kind of crap anymore. We're a big
company now,
selling games all over the world, way outside the niche markets we
started in.
We have a duty to represent ourselves as a mature company that is
sensitive
to the political, religious, gender, and ethnic issues that are facing
society
today. This change is in response to that duty.

We could lose millions of dollars over this decision.

I don't care. We have to what we think is right.

Mavra!
(Peter D. Adkison, Janitor, Wizards of the Coast, Inc.)
-~-~-~-~-~-~-~-~-~-

>
> Fred

Kevin M., Prince of Madison, WI

Going back to what I brought up earlier, I recall that the comparision
of ww doing single print cards to e-books was made.

This should have been a reference to the current Book printing
technology being developed that allows publishers to print 'A' book on
demand, thus virtually eliminating having to maintain any inventory.

With out any good tech facts ect. I hereby postulate.

If WW were to set up, train 2-3 people to run a printing machine, and
they spent 250K doing so,how long might it take to generate a profit.

Take care to remember that currently a single card sells for .25c US.
This is the price out of the pack. On this .25c per card WW makes
suitable profit to continue doing sales in card packs.

Out of this .25c you must remove the cost for the printing company, you
have to remove the cost for the distributer, and you have to remove the
cost that the store owner gets. So without going into a few other
nibles into that .25c per card, you have WW getting 1/4 of the value of
a card. 6c.

Now if the print on demand cards were a completely new and different set
of cards, and also had the avialablity of old cards, they could do cards
of high power, and simply charge 50$ each.

Of course I do not support high powered cards simple to generate $$, but
take that 250K figure. if currently unavailable rare card were sold at
5$ each on a order to order basis, they would completely break even
after 50,000 cards.

If you take this as a multiple year investment, say over 5 years, then
250K needs to be increased by the 3 employees printing cards, say 80K a
year, time 5 years, or 400K. This gets you 650K in costs to be
recovered. So 26,000 cards each year breaks even and anything over that
becomes profit.

Of course this does not taking into account a lot of variables,
depreciation, retraining blah, blah,blah, ect ect ect.

So, this print on demand is feasable and currently available with
standard technology.

It can be done, IF it wants to be done. Costs could be shifted away
from WW by utilizing the printer and their equipment, especially a
printer already getting into the print on demand book market.

It is feasably, and it is afforadable. The only reason it has not been
done yet is that it requires a new train og thought, a new marketing
schedule and most importantly, the ability to LEAD.

Messages.Author: Jason Bell
Messages.Body:
"XZealot" <X_Ze...@bellsouth.net> wrote

> Jason,
> Please address these 4 points and I am sure the rest of the gang will

Don't be so sure, but anyway...

I didn't ask anyone to leave me alone, I just encouraged those
who responded to address my arguments. For space and
clarity, I'm going to address most of these questions exclusively
for the selling of sets, as that seems to be where the discussion
currently stands (the "by title" part of this debate is over for
me, as I have conceded that it may well be impossible for WW to
do profitably, but other interesting arguments have popped
up especially relating to booster size, rarity to commons ratios,
even the elimination of a rare sheet altogether)

Before I begin in earnest, let me say that The Nosferatu Stuff
beat me to the punch in responding to this, and though I will try
to address these nonetheless, I'll try to avoid overly re-hashing
his post, with which I agree for the most part.

> These are a few of many possible reasons that WW during its successful
> resurrection of a dead game that was a failure to successfully make
> money yet a very fun game refuses to reprint sorted sets of cards.
>
> 1) depression of demand for boosters.

I have conceded that any new card distribution method
must reduce demand for boosters. The longtime existence
of starters did this, and the distribution of pre-constructed
decks do the same.

My question is whether an additional distribution scheme
(my suggestion being sets) would increase total product
sales or not. If sets depress total demand for cards, this
would be a strong argument for avoiding selling sets (though
not neccessarily a complete argument, depending on why
total demand would be depressed; after all, if demand
diminished only to the extent that consumers no longer
bought cards they did not need and could not use, selling
sets with the result of decreased demand could still be a
good idea)

One solution I offered for consideration for dealing with
fear of decreased total demand is to delay set availability
until some time after initial booster availability, which seems
like the safest bet for increasing total sales by offering product
when booster sales would presumably be at or near their nadir.

> 2) increased costs of production.

I have conceded that increased production costs are a
very strong reason indeed for White Wolf to not Ventrue
into the market of selling individual cards on demand by title.

However, no such argument can be made against the selling
of sets. By selling sets, an extra manufacturing step
can be completely avoided (where cards are randomized),
and entire sheets can be cut then immediately packaged
for sale. Overall, this seems like it would decrease costs
of production. I would be mightily curious to know whether
it is cheaper per card for WW to produce its pre-con
decks or cards in the old starter format. That seems like
information which would settle this point rather decicively.

> 3) marginal increase in utility to players who vastly outnumber
> collectors

I thought I had gone through several arguments for how
players would benefit from set availability. In general,
those arguments involved 1. The stabilization of the
secondary markets for individual cards; or B. Envisioned
a route for players to acquire a card or cards they want by
buying them from WW, with a known ceiling for the cost and
reduced uncertainty of receiving the sought card(s).

But perhaps I misinterpret your definition of collector
as opposed to player. If I seek specific card or cards
to play in a deck, I assume you would call me a player, yes?
It is a very difficult distinction, as I imagine very small
exclusive areas in the Venn diagram.

> 4) If it ain't broken, don't fix it.

My original criticism of White Wolf makes plain
my opinion that I believe that it is broken.

The way this game is sold is terribly wasteful, and inneficient
to the point where a secondary market is generated to
distribute its game pieces to both players and collectors.
As far as I know, such markets do not exist for non TCGs,
unless those games are no longer produced by their
manufacturer.

It very well may be that "it ain't broken" from WW's
financial standpoint, and perhaps offering consumers
another way to buy the cards from the manufacturer
would destroy the game by some mechanism that is
unknown to me, but I have yet to hear a thoughtful
argument as to how.

Anyway, that's my response to your four major
areas. I don't claim that these responses fully
resolve any of the four issues you stated, but
I hope they demonstrate that my opinions on the
matter are not thoughtless, mindless, or
ill-considered, as has been suggested by my
detractor.

- Jason Bell

> > 1) depression of demand for boosters.
>
> I have conceded that any new card distribution method
> must reduce demand for boosters. The longtime existence
> of starters did this, and the distribution of pre-constructed
> decks do the same.
>
> My question is whether an additional distribution scheme
> (my suggestion being sets) would increase total product
> sales or not. If sets depress total demand for cards, this
> would be a strong argument for avoiding selling sets (though
> not neccessarily a complete argument, depending on why
> total demand would be depressed; after all, if demand
> diminished only to the extent that consumers no longer
> bought cards they did not need and could not use, selling
> sets with the result of decreased demand could still be a
> good idea)
>
> One solution I offered for consideration for dealing with
> fear of decreased total demand is to delay set availability
> until some time after initial booster availability, which seems
> like the safest bet for increasing total sales by offering product
> when booster sales would presumably be at or near their nadir.
>

How does the market demand this product? If as you say you delay the
issuing of complete sets until after the initial rush of booster
collecting,
then certainly wouldn't you eliminate from the potential customer
group those
customers who have already put together a set.

> > 2) increased costs of production.
>
> I have conceded that increased production costs are a
> very strong reason indeed for White Wolf to not Ventrue
> into the market of selling individual cards on demand by title.
>
> However, no such argument can be made against the selling
> of sets. By selling sets, an extra manufacturing step
> can be completely avoided (where cards are randomized),
> and entire sheets can be cut then immediately packaged
> for sale. Overall, this seems like it would decrease costs
> of production.

I would argue with you there. I am have been in the manufacturing
business for about 18 years. Manufacturing profitably is setting up
a specialized multi-step process to create goods at a affordable cost.
If you package sets then you are not packaging boosters. To justify
your changing of the packaging process to sets, you must be able to
prove before you change that you can make money doing so. Otherwise,
there is a real possibility of losing money. No established
businessman
would enter into such a venture without very real market data showing
that it would be profitable.

> > 3) marginal increase in utility to players who vastly outnumber
> > collectors
>
> I thought I had gone through several arguments for how
> players would benefit from set availability. In general,
> those arguments involved 1. The stabilization of the
> secondary markets for individual cards; or B. Envisioned
> a route for players to acquire a card or cards they want by
> buying them from WW, with a known ceiling for the cost and
> reduced uncertainty of receiving the sought card(s).
>
> But perhaps I misinterpret your definition of collector
> as opposed to player. If I seek specific card or cards
> to play in a deck, I assume you would call me a player, yes?
> It is a very difficult distinction, as I imagine very small
> exclusive areas in the Venn diagram.

I defined neither collector nor player. For the purposes of this
arguement they are mutually excusive. A collector collects the
cards with no intrest in playability, merely in resale value. A
players collects the cards for playability with no intrest in
resale value.

To address your point, didn't you say above (under point 1)
that the selling of singles by WW would be by definition unprofitable
at any reasonable price. I do not believe that players will spend
$100 dollars for
a set (this is a hypothetical price) just to aquire one to ten cards.
They
will have already spent between $200 to $300 dollars to buy boosters
for play
stock. So that leaves collectors. I have no idea how many VTES
collectors
we have out there. So if as you say the printing of the sets puts a
ceiling on
the value of cards wouldn't that dissuade collecters from buying
either boosters
or the set because the value of their cards will never increase beyond
a certain
point.

> > 4) If it ain't broken, don't fix it.
>
> My original criticism of White Wolf makes plain
> my opinion that I believe that it is broken.
>
> The way this game is sold is terribly wasteful, and inneficient
> to the point where a secondary market is generated to
> distribute its game pieces to both players and collectors.
> As far as I know, such markets do not exist for non TCGs,
> unless those games are no longer produced by their
> manufacturer.

ROTFLOL, whew! that's a good one. Stop it. My sides hurt.
The key word here is as far as you know. You don't know.
Scrye has printed a Collectible Card Game Price Guide for
for what I can tell is every single card game ever printed.
It is as thick as your phonebook/Bible. In addition
to VTES, it has in its pages everysingle expansion for Magic,
Legend of the 5 Rings, even Netrunner, and so many more. This
guide is the card collector's "Bible" it gives you a general idea
for demand for any one card. It is actual physcial proof that
secondary markets exist for other card games.

>
> It very well may be that "it ain't broken" from WW's
> financial standpoint, and perhaps offering consumers
> another way to buy the cards from the manufacturer
> would destroy the game by some mechanism that is
> unknown to me, but I have yet to hear a thoughtful
> argument as to how.

Let me explain it to you. The mechanism is called capitalism.
You produce a product at a cost. You then sell it for more
than that cost. The difference is called Profit. Profit can be
either negitive or positive. Negative Profits are called Losses.
Losses are bad as they eat up the supply of money you have. This
is not a good thing.

Alternitive means of purchasing from White Wolf would be bad.
My piddling purchase of $250 dollars from a distributor is nice
if it is matched by 100 other orders for that same amount. So
for White Wolf that single distributor bought $25,000 worth of product
on one order. They only have to process that one order. This
costs signifigantly less than having to process 100 orders.
You want to eliminate the middleman (i.e. the distributor) but
yet you cannot eliminate his function (the warehousing and processing
of individual customer's orders). We also have to take into account
that the $25,000 includes the distributor's profit. So let's take a
profit
margin of 30% for the distributor. So now that is only $17,500 in
revenue
for WW. Now White Wolf is outsourcing their manufacturing of VTES,
and
the cost of cards to be printed is $2,500. That leaves $15,000 dollars
left
over. Now you have to pay the creative staff who creates the cards
and
artwork. So lets say that this is a 3 month project. That is $5,000
dollars
a month they have to spend. That is 4 people making $1,250.00 per
month before
taxes. This is all before you have processed one order.

Do you understand?

>
> Anyway, that's my response to your four major
> areas. I don't claim that these responses fully
> resolve any of the four issues you stated, but
> I hope they demonstrate that my opinions on the
> matter are not thoughtless, mindless, or
> ill-considered, as has been suggested by my
> detractor.

I believe that you have a good head on your shoulders, and you have
been both the victim and the progenitor of many of these flames. My
problem is that I do not think you have taken the real world
considerations
into play before you make your points. And yes, I was incredibly
offended
by your characterization of WW as a evil company that fleeces its
customers.



By simple economic law you have created a substitute, and substitutes
decrease demand. In the real world, you try never ever to compete
with yourself. It is bad for business unless you own the whole
market. By printing sets you are
creating an item that competes for customers with your regular booster
stock.

Not necessarily full sorted sets, read any of my posts for

We already have non-complete set for sale. They are called

> 2. There is no increase in production. If white wolf packaged a full sheet

There might not be any increase in production. You are going to have

"different schemes of distribution" in a different manner. This costs

manufacturing process to create the
"different scheme of distribution". Change is bad for manufacturing.
Change causes costs to increase. Cost eat profits. Profits pay
workers. Workers
do the work that makes the product. Do you see how changing the
"distribution scheme" would increase costs so that they could afford
less workers which would lower the quality of the end product, not to
mention the quantity of end product that could be produced at a
profit.

> 3. Okay. I believe you have provided valid points for why sets are not a
> good idea. None of them seem to disprove why they are a potentially good
> idea, but there are two sides to every topic.

The single biggest hurdle that the Pro-Set group has to clear is "How
does printing a set increase the overall demand for my product without
signifigantly decreasing the demand for an identical product that I
already manufacture?"

> 4. The game wasn't broke after V:TES.

It was broke. Distributors were going broke for buying it. Let's
see, at one point in time you could buy boxes of Jyhad for $5.00.
They cost the distributor $20.00. That is a loss of $15.00 on every
box. That is going broke about as fast as you can.

It isn't broke now.

Then why do you want to change it?

There was
> nothing broken with random starter decks.

LOL, that's a good one. have you ever just bought a Jyhad or VTES
started and tried to play with it. You can't. It is incohesive. If
you are lucky two vampires will be from the same clan. The random
starters for Jyhad/VTES were awful. No one could start playing the
game right out of the box. It was a bunch of cards that required
diffent things that were in short supply.

There was no need for the
> preconstructed.

Are you on crack? Okay I will stop with the flames. How do you get
new players interested in the game? You construct a deck and you give
it to them. The Starters should have already done that. They didn't.
So now we have pre-cons.
They were very necessary.

They are a nice addition.

I think if nice was an abbreviation for necessary than I would agree
with you.

There are possibly other things
> that would be helpful as well. Maybe we could figure them out if it wasn't
> for the: "Screw you" and "Screw you more" bantering of certain people on
> this thread. Any good system needs to be shaken up every so often. If
> there is nothing broken, then we need no new cards. No new sets. Nothing.
> No progress is made by sitting idle.

This is a game, not social engineering. People should be allowed to
fight. It is entertaining.

Progress is made within the context of the game. Think Chess.

> > and entire sheets can be cut then immediately packaged
> > for sale. Overall, this seems like it would decrease costs
> > of production.
>
> I would argue with you there. I am have been in the manufacturing
> business for about 18 years. Manufacturing profitably is setting up
> a specialized multi-step process to create goods at a affordable cost.
> If you package sets then you are not packaging boosters.

Pre-con decks are a different multi-stage process than boosters,
and that doesn't seem to cause WW undue difficulty, despite
conforming to the above objections.

> To justify
> your changing of the packaging process to sets, you must be able to
> prove before you change that you can make money doing so. Otherwise,
> there is a real possibility of losing money. No established
> businessman
> would enter into such a venture without very real market data showing
> that it would be profitable.

Of course, if this observation were always true (though I agree
that such sedentary conservatism exists in business), there would
probably never have been a TCG industry at all. I wouldn't be
shocked if there were WW people who would take a swing at
you if you described them to be the above businessmen.

> I defined neither collector nor player. For the purposes of this
> arguement they are mutually excusive. A collector collects the
> cards with no intrest in playability, merely in resale value. A
> players collects the cards for playability with no intrest in
> resale value.

That's a tough model, particularly since I don't know anyone
who falls into it. There probably are exclusive collectors,
but the only exclusive players I know don't own cards, or
at least don't buy them anymore. They borrow mine.

> To address your point, didn't you say above (under point 1)
> that the selling of singles by WW would be by definition unprofitable
> at any reasonable price.

No, I did not say that.
I concede that the logistics of WW entering the singles market
would involve a great deal of complexity and uncertainty, such
that I won't argue that WW should do it.

> I do not believe that players will spend $100 dollars for
> a set (this is a hypothetical price) just to aquire one to ten cards.

If it's just one to ten cards, of course you are correct, but
it's probably like one to ten cards that the player really wants,
plus maybe 30 others or more that the player would not mind
having more of. As an exercise, browse the Final Nights
checklist to see if this correlates with your preferences.

> So that leaves collectors. I have no idea how many VTES
> collectors
> we have out there. So if as you say the printing of the sets puts a
> ceiling on
> the value of cards wouldn't that dissuade collecters from buying
> either boosters
> or the set because the value of their cards will never increase beyond
> a certain point.

I guess I just disagree with this, I think players would buy
the sets. But just as important, the secondary market becomes
much more efficient when the inputs are known with certainty.
This allows better distribution of individual game pieces in the
face of the idea that WW may not be able to sell singles
without great risk.

> > > 4) If it ain't broken, don't fix it.
> >
> > My original criticism of White Wolf makes plain
> > my opinion that I believe that it is broken.
> >
> > The way this game is sold is terribly wasteful, and inneficient
> > to the point where a secondary market is generated to
> > distribute its game pieces to both players and collectors.
> > As far as I know, such markets do not exist for non TCGs,
> > unless those games are no longer produced by their
> > manufacturer.
>
> ROTFLOL, whew! that's a good one. Stop it. My sides hurt.
> The key word here is as far as you know. You don't know.
> Scrye has printed a Collectible Card Game Price Guide for
> for what I can tell is every single card game ever printed.
> It is as thick as your phonebook/Bible.

Right, you can stop laughing, as I'm assuming that all
those price lists are for card games, as I described
above. My point was that secondary markets are a
function of the trading card industry. Did Scrye
even exist before Magic? If it did, I imagine that
it was not a pricing guide for collectibles.

> It is actual physcial proof that
> secondary markets exist for other card games.

I never claimed otherwise. But to illustrate my point,
you'll probably not find the price of a Monopoly hotel on
any such list. Similar lists do exist for antiques and
other collectibles, but the only such collectible that
I know had such a list while it was manufactured were
Beanie Babies. I suppose used autos have the same
types of lists, but stess on the word "used."

> > It very well may be that "it ain't broken" from WW's
> > financial standpoint, and perhaps offering consumers
> > another way to buy the cards from the manufacturer
> > would destroy the game by some mechanism that is
> > unknown to me, but I have yet to hear a thoughtful
> > argument as to how.
>
> Let me explain it to you. The mechanism is called capitalism.
> You produce a product at a cost. You then sell it for more
> than that cost. The difference is called Profit. Profit can be
> either negitive or positive. Negative Profits are called Losses.
> Losses are bad as they eat up the supply of money you have. This
> is not a good thing.

Stage 1: Collect Underpants
Stage 3: Profit

> [snip]
> Do you understand?

Not at all, I am unclear as to why set sales cannot
flow through the same distributors as the other
packaged merchandise. I don't think I ever attacked
the manufacturer-to-retailer distribution scheme,
just the randomly distributed cards-in-packs
distribution scheme. Apologies if that was unclear.

> My problem is that I do not think you have taken the real
> world considerations into play before you make your points.

Well, I've been a consumer of Deckmaster products for
a long time (ever since the middle of The Dark print run
for M:tG). I've bought M:tG, Jyhad, and watched my
friends buy any number of other games in the industry
(Netrunner, L5R, even Dragon Dice), and also been a
consumer of many traditional box games.

I've seen both the good and the bad sides of Magic as
its creators-cum-businessmen took the game through
its growing pains and inflicted some of those pains on its
customers. I've watched the development of the entire
TCG industry from inception to boom to shake out to
where it is now.

The ideas I've discussed in this thread have,
in many cases, been expressions of the real world lessons
those observations taught me, ideas of how some of the
serious shortcomings of a novel game format could be
addressed.

So no, I believe I have had at least one foot in the
real world during this discussion, and where I have
strayed, I have at least been within sight of the
real world.

> And yes, I was incredibly offended by your characterization
> of WW as a evil company that fleeces its customers.

When White Wolf inherits V:tES from WotC and continues WotC's
TCG distribution model for its expansions, it exposes itself to the
same criticisms to which WotC gets criticized (at least in kind,
whether or not in extent).

Look back at the early posts in this thread, several took WotC as an
example of the 'real' or 'worse' bad guys and got no criticism for
those claims, then consider the functional differences between the
two companies in regards to Final Nights as compared to, say,
Magic: Mercadian Masques products.

Perhaps I could have used some more flowery language, but
I used the term in the post to which I was responding, so
there you go.

But yeah, if you want to be incredibly offended, the
internet is definitely the place to be. 8-)

- Jason Bell

On Sun, 22 Jul 2001 18:10:54 GMT, Robert Goudie wrote:

>We are aware that his problems were "secondary" concerns. However, you should
>remember that we were all working hard to support the game and to show there was
>a market for the product. This task becomes rather pointless when someone tells
>you that it doesn't matter how successful you are at generating interest, etc.
>because they won't meet the demand with product no matter what you do.

He was not closing the door forever and said:

>We are,however, planning to get some better support for Vampire
>players in terms of Organized Play at cons this summer, and a
>better and more responsive internal team for answering rules questions.

>As one of the most successful TCGs ever, Vampire has a special place in the
>hearts of many people here at WotC. While it is not a part of our current
>design plans, we do respect deeply the people who have invested in the game...
>...
>However, we continue to monitor the market and to talk about the brand, and if the
>company makes the decision at some point to reawaken the beast, we'll ensure
>that you're the first people to know.

Compared with what happens to most CCG when they fail, this was
comparatively generous. But this wasn't good enough for you and so
you started this morality crap (which he hadn't mentioned), trying to
blacken the name of his other games. When you started baiting him
about the supposed immorality of the samurai in L5R, he naturally
defended it. He never said or suggested that he was actively
suppressing VTES for this reason - the primary reason for keeping it
on hold was that it hadn't been meeting his minimum sales requirements
and he didn't see any prospect of it doing so.

>Yep. Mostly just a bunch of fanboys...oh, and some higher-ups at WotC.

These "higher-ups" may have got excited when he observed that Magic
had dubious morality too. They would be the same higher-ups that
released precisely zero new product for VTES in 1997 - a clear kiss of
death. Ryan was now announcing production plans for 1998. These
higher-ups were privy to those plans and approved them. They might
have been hoping that he'd pull some rabbit out the hat for VTES (and
Netrunner) but, given that they had so singularly failed to do so
themselves, could hardly complain if he left these products as he
found them. And bear in mind that he was announcing new product for 9
other games - a plan which was already ambitious (over ambitious, as
it proved).

No, the people who screwed the game up were the WotC mainstream,
especially those who were responsible for it after the initial release
of Jyhad. It was they who decided to print no further sets after
Sabbat. I expect the main reason they don't get all this wrath
directed at them is that no senior person ever bothered to communicate
with you and so your anger and frustration had no target until Ryan
came along.

Andrew

You missed out:

"Ah, letter H. For VtES fans, "H" might as well stand for "Hold" which
is where VtES is in terms of future expansions. There is no chance for
a VtES product in 1998, and virtually no chance for new VtES in 1999."

In the context of his later comments, this meant to everyone I saw
responding:

- Nothing in '98. Nothing in '99.

Quite *why* this was so is uncertain. White Wolf have shown that, even
without the WotC juggernaut pushing it, V:TES has more than enough
demand for it to justify the effort - which would mostly amount to: 3
(say) staff-members working with LSJ to create card texts and acting as
a Design Team for that expansion, co-ordinating play-testing and
commissioning art. With a sensible finance department, this can all be
recouped. Indeed, WotC *did* show that they wanted to do something
similar before the game reverted to White Wolf (some of the discussions
regarding the renewal of the licence from White Wolf, the subsequent
decision to licence the Deckmaster technology to White Wolf and the
decision for WotC to drop their support for the game were done at a high
enough level that some of the people doing the stuff on the floor didn't
know (apparently) what was going on). Suggestions of a mini expansion,
with a single sheet for each of V:TES, Netrunner and Spellfire (I think
it was those three) were mooted. Display boxes with a third of each
were also suggested. (A number of people murmured about this. V:TES
had specific areas of support, in the US and Europe. Spellfire was
still going strong in parts of Germany. Netrunner was, presumably,
similarly successful somewhere - not following the game, I couldn't
say.)

The concept of recycling art to keep costs down low was also suggested.
With Netrunner and Rage both being around at WotC, various cyber-punk
techno-elements could have been sourced that way. I imagine it wouldn't
be terribly difficult to have asked that nice, cuddly Mr. Wieck if he
wouldn't mind terribly letting you borrow a few pieces of artwork for a
small fee (and a fee to the artist, of course, which would most likely
be reduced for another printing, rather than original commission).

Playtesting wouldn't be terribly hard. With someone like LSJ actively
involved, it wouldn't be terribly difficult to shuffle off most of the
work to him. If you set up closed mailing lists for playtesters,
allowing them to communicate with one another to try and speed the whole
evolution process along ("Wow, you can do that with Augustus' Cigar
Case?" "Yup, and just think about how that interacts with Daytime
Slumber!" "Oh jees, you guys, do that with that new ally Donatello
(Ninja Turtle) and just think of what can happen." - such things happen
more slowly in isolated groups) and then get the three staff members to
sit down and read it on, say, a Friday afternoon, issuing a Playtesters
Rules Team statement, card text changes and such like, it doesn't take a
whole lot of work.

Promoting Magic as the key game at the time (and potentially Pokémon)
was understandable. The world paper market was going stupid. The
number of slots you could get at a printers/collators for doing thing
like Magic was similarly small, comparatively. You couldn't afford to
"waste" a slot you had at the printers, or waste card stock.

That Netrunner was promoted above V:TES in line of production raised a
large number of eyebrows. Some of this was, of course, minor jealousy,
but a lot of it was "Erm, but guys, Netrunner just doesn't sell that
well, from all our forays (and V:TES has a fairly global network of
players, even if there is localised strong support in a number of
areas). If you put your toe in the water with Netrunner, you're going
to fight it positively luke warm at best."

V:TES was a game that was selling out sets of Sabbat. 1st printing sold
out. 2nd printing sold extremely well too. This showed there was
demand. That the game had only just broken even on this level of demand
generally showed that someone at WotC had Messed Up (tm). However, the
demand was not only there, it could be seen to be there.

But sure, V:TES gets put back a bit. We understand, you have to do what
you think is best for business reasons. However:

- Dancey's subsequent outbursts and refusal to address a large number of
points raised in a manner which addressed the actual substance of the
holes being pointed out set the wrong tone. V:TES wasn't getting any
(card) support in '98 and '99. That's dealable with. When you have a
manager who is setting a tone of "And I *won't* be supporting this game
at all, because it's evil" (which is the tone he was setting and doing
*nothing* to counteract) the suggestion is very much that it doesn't
matter what business arguments you put to him, he won't act on business
matters. When that's his *job*, he assembles his own noose as far as
that line is concerned.

Let's let the game speak for itself:

"Welcome to Rage, the collectible trading card game based on the
storytelling game Werewolf: The Apocalypse. Each Rage player controls
a pack of savage and heroic werewolves (called Garou). Garou packs
often unite to combat the evil force known as the Wyrm, but equally
often battle one another for the ultimate position of pack dominance.
A pack achieves victory by conquering the Wyrm, by overpowering rival
Garou, or performing heroic tasks."

much as Pokemon is about as moral as cock-fighting - you find exotic
creatures in the wild and train them to fight each other for your
gratification and glory.

>Talons like to eat people, for example.

That's no random example - they are the Garou hard-liners. There are
nasty Pokemon too.

>the car.

WW have taken a low-cost approach to the game - fan labour, cheap
recycled art, small print runs, no licence fee. This is similar to
what Z-Man have done with Shadowfist and it's the only way that games
like this can keep going. It's not the business that WotC was in.
It's kinda like going to a back-street garage rather than a main
dealer.

Andrew

immoral". It's nice that you at least can see something good about

you must see that there's a problem with somebody who says "i'm
canning this game for commercial reasons" and then, when those
commercial reasons are questioned on logical grounds, changes his
response to "alright, whatever the commercial facts of the matter i'm
STILL going to can this game because i find it repugnant". i'm just
baffled by your apparent belief that we should admire and defer to his
commercial judgement in respect of CCGs AND his moral position on
VTES, given that both were/are, quite obviously, questionable. And as
for DnD, well, that was a success before Dancey, and it still is. Good
luck to it! Because Mrs Thatcher won the Falklands war and oversaw the
successful building of the Channel Tunnel, does it follow that
everything she did whilst Prime Minister was a Good Thing, would you
say?

are NOT admirable, but i think it's a stretch from there to say that
VTES is immoral. A major, perhaps THE major thread in VtM AND VTES is
the quest for redemption from evil - cf Golconda, Humanitas, Atonement
and Return to Innocence. Monsters we are, lest monsters we become is
the slogan, isn't it? And while it admits of all sorts of
interpretations, total moral blindness can't easily be counted among
them, i'ld suggest. The flip side of this coin is the self-righteous
and hormonally-challenged werewolves who, whatever their ostensible
motivation, are actually busy dragging down everything they're
supposed to be protecting by their pride and, yes, moral blindness to
the truth that the end does NOT justify the means.

Yup. However, at the time, as I recall, the feelings went like this:

Pre-Dancey:

*sigh* WotC are just leaving V:TES alone. If we go hard enough, we
might get them to re-print Sabbat. But it just plain sucks, you know?
We can do whatever we want to prove that it's a perfectly viable,
profitable game and they just won't listen!

So, what about if we lobby for them to sell it on, or just imagine it as
wishful thinking? Who'd be good? Well, FRPG might be good. They can
be committed to fans, they can work well with plotted backgrounds, they
can produce well-tested products which aren't about milking players dry.

Newsflash: Wizards buy FRPG

Oh bugger.

Newsflash: FRPG given internal responsibility for V:TES

Woo.

Then a few people wonder about the product guidelines (which when the
buy-out etc. was going on, most of us didn't even *know* about, I'd
guess) and everything happens as detailed.

During the whole thing, a few mentions were made at a number of points
about a White Wolf buy-out. This raised a number of difficult points:

- their card games blew chunks as, to coin a term, SCGs (strategic card
games)
- they seemed to have shuffled all their card games off (Rage had just
been sold on to FRPG, Changeling was being (rightfully) ignored
</troll> - Legbiter will be along in a second to defend it ;-) )
- would they have the muscle to pull something off in, effectively, an
entirely new world for them?

I think a lot of us *hoped* they'd do it well, but equally feared it
could go wrong.

When the entire licence switch thing happened (which took everyone on
the ground, without a friendly spy wherever, by surprise), I think the
fact that White Wolf showed within the following month, say:

- we'll listen to players;
- we're going to actually learn and play the game ourselves;
- we're going to keep LSJ on *and* keep him heavily involved;
- Steve Wieck will not be some aloof CEO (I don't know what his actual
title is, sorry), he'll actually respond every now and then to
your concerns personally;
- we want to back you up with prize support;
- we're not going to do Rage II and scrap everything;
- we're going to be sensible and just do a small expansion (in terms of
*new* cards first);

and so on, it exceeded our wildest expectations of what was possible.

I can honestly say that when the whole FRPG ideas were mooted, then FRPG
was bought on, then we were allocated to FRPG, I don't know anyone who
believed that WW could make as good a go of it as they have.

We got lucky and I'm very grateful that we did. But I don't think
anyone expected it at the time.

Messages.Author: Lemar Johnson
Messages.Body:
Andrew S. Davidson <a...@csi.com> wrote in message news:<4C7C56AB2E2681FE.71506271...@lp.airnews.net>...
> On 19 Jul 2001 04:09:06 -0700, legbiter wrote:

> >VtES: You are evil
> >Rage: You fight against evil
> >Comprende?
>
> Having looked at Rage now, this is a fair point - the Garou are heroic
> defenders of Gaia against the servants of the evil Wyrm - Pentex, the
> Vampires etc.
>

Whew. A bit of digression here -- I apologize if I offend by the
subject modification.

Rage is not about a bunch of heroic werewolves. Werewolves are not
heroes. They are monsters. They are not nice to people. They serve
their own interests as callously as any corporate raider. This is seen
clearly in the source material, but also in the card game as well.

Make no mistake, the foe they were designed to face (via plot) is the
Wyrm, which is almost completely evil. (I say almost completely as it
has gone mad and its victims are not always of sound mind, but its
direct emanations can be considered, in a cartoonish sense, to have no
unredeeming features.) Nevertheless, the Garou are themselves
responsible for the elevation of the Wyrm in the modern day. The Garou
slaughtered humanity mercilessly in antiquity (so the story goes),
impressing the Delirium upon humanity and encouraging them to cut
themselves off from matters of the spirit, driving them to the Weaver.
To make a long, complicated (and not a little contradictory) story
short, they are responsible for the modern day problems -- they
damaged the very heart of humanity with the Impergium.

And what do they do now? Fight and kill each other as much as anyone
else. They slaughter their own kind into nigh-extinction, exacerbating
problems with their shrinking wildernesses. One entire tribe was
slaughtered to a man due to Garou lust for territory.

In the card game, you get most of your victory points (needed to win)
from slaughtering your opponent's Garou. In fact, the default state of
the game is that our Garou fight, and occasionally a Wyrm enemy
appears, at which point we fight each other and it.

Both L5R and Rage feature relatively amoral societies. L5R features an
entire underclass used as slave labor for their betters and casual
death of subordinates for the pleasure of the ruling elite -- just
like any feudal background. Rage features a group of terrifying,
sentient monsters with human drives. These are not nice people.

Vampire presents us with a group of ancient vampires who manipulate
other vampires. Though it's very likely that they or their pawns do
bad things, there's nothing to suggest that what they do is anything
near the scale of L5R. Jyhad is a very abstract game -- today's
session could be about who gets control of Mexico or who gets control
over this Rembrant painting I and Methuselah B over there have been
arguing over for centuries. I'm not saying that vampires are good, but
I am saying that trying to call one's role in the other card games out
there "good" and the role one plays in VtES "bad" is an absurd thing.
I must respectfully disagree with such a notion.

-- Lemar Johnson

> Let's let the game speak for itself:
>
> "Welcome to Rage, the collectible trading card game based on the
> storytelling game Werewolf: The Apocalypse. Each Rage player controls
> a pack of savage and heroic werewolves (called Garou). Garou packs
> often unite to combat the evil force known as the Wyrm, but equally
> often battle one another for the ultimate position of pack dominance.
> A pack achieves victory by conquering the Wyrm, by overpowering rival
> Garou, or performing heroic tasks."

Note, again, that the vast majority of the time in the card game is
spent not merely "battling one another for the ultimate position of
pack dominance" but slaughtering each other for the win. This is not a
matter of wolves struggling to be alpha. Losing Garou end up *dead*.
The winners in the card game generally rule a kingdom of corpses.

And the roleplaying game, which is the primary source for the card
game, does nothing to suggest that the Garou are caring creatures.
Hell, the Shadow Lords are second only in power to the decrepit Silver
Fangs, and they are legendary for working with vampires. And the
latter are usually put in the "unreedemably evil" department by Garou.

Legbiter is right; despite the text you mentioned, the game itself is
not about heroes fighting a morally wrong enemy. It is about social,
political, and military power struggles.

> It's more morally uplifting than Pokemon, IMO. Not that that's saying
> much as Pokemon is about as moral as cock-fighting - you find exotic
> creatures in the wild and train them to fight each other for your
> gratification and glory.

There is nothing morally uplifting about either. Poekemon is animal
abuse. Rage features the destruction of property and loss of human
life to further the goals of a few metahumans. Ah -- that sounds
familiar. One could apply that statement to a certain game about the
undead...

> >Werewolves are morally neutral, to put it at it kindest. The Red
> >Talons like to eat people, for example.
>
> That's no random example - they are the Garou hard-liners. There are
> nasty Pokemon too.

The Garou are not neutral. They are self-interested. Some individuals
do good things, some bad. However, all individuals have a berserk fury
and a nigh-unstoppable physical form which means, just like with
vampires, they usually end up murdering people in the course of their
existence even if they're not "mean people." White Wolf claims that
Werewolf and Vampire are games where you play monsters; this is
accurate.

Modern hobby games are *not* good places to develop ethical rigor and
ethical comparisons between White Wolf products is a little silly, to
say the least. They can be lots of fun, though.

-- Lemar Johnson

The first question has an ambiguous answer, the second does not.
Players enjoyed playing Wyrm, though they found them woefully
underpowered. Plus, a series of bad rulings neutered them in
non-thematic ways (Black Spiral Dancers were cut off from Auspice
Gifts, despite world background says on the issue.)

The expansion wasn't much of a success, mostly because it was bereft
with rules problems. Constantly. I have documents showing a set of
three reversals on just one essential rules issue ("can Wyrm creatures
be affected by negative Enemy effects"). Players had difficulty with
the base rules and those were *still* being revised and, occasionally,
arbitrarily changed. White Wolf seemed committed to making what Tweet
wanted to be a very simple game become a morass of rules problems. (To
which Tweet was the initial source, admittedly -- you could not play a
clear game of Rage from the first set with the original rulebook, due
to ambiguity.)

The expansion sold cards and made a profit, to be sure, but it did not
endear itself to its fan base, from what I understand

-- Lemar Johnson

> >killing the game.
>
> This sort of thing, however, works to undermine one of Jyhad's founding
> principles - that any given card should be usable in a deck up to the
> maximum deck limit. In a game where you can only use 1 (in the case of
> a number of games with Uniques with 1/deck limits) or 4 or 5, selling
> limited run sets isn't such a problem. Jyhad internally handles such
> issues very, very differently.

> Out of interest (having played Lo5R once or twice, never really getting
> into it, and finding it a bit like creating a table-cloth out of cards
> at times), how many of that set were Uniques, Events or Experienced (he
> said, fiddling with an old rulebook), such that only 1 could be used?
> I'm guessing the proportion is fairly high, so I'd be interested to be
> proved wrong.

Everything in HoR was Unique, by necessity. It was a small set (20
cards) and was sold in a very, very limited print run. If it had
featured many non-Unique cards, it would have been an utter insult to
players. The vast majority of L5R players would not have a single copy
of these cards, while others could have enough to fill decks with
duplicates (up to three are legal in a deck). This decision, to only
make Unique cards in the set, was a necessity that resulted from the
poor decisions (IMHO) to make it an exclusive one -- a "reward" for
members of the Imperial Assembly. A reward that costed $80. As I said,
it wasn't the happiest example. But people did buy it completely out,
and the secondary market benefited from it, and it did not adversely
affect booster or starter sales in any way.

-- Lemar Johnson

Messages.Author: Lemar Johnson
Messages.Body:
Andrew S. Davidson <a...@csi.com> wrote in message news:<43772D9B4DAA5A85.CE745567...@lp.airnews.net>...
> On 20 Jul 2001 20:39:51 -0700, Lemar Johnson wrote:
>
> >Still (to go beyond speaking of INWO or Rolling Thunder), I have seen
> >no examples of the reprint of a card in any game -- especially when
> >the reprint is in a different format (color or art changes, for
> >example) -- having a detrimental effect on the singles market, even
> >less the set sales itself. The value of the original card for
> >collectors was in its rarity, not its playability.
>
> How about:
>
> Ting Ting in Shadowfist
> The Drifter in Doomtown
> Dreams of the Sphynx in VTES
>
> These were all highly prized rares which were subsequently reprinted
> as fixed cards in starters. The Netherworld Ting Ting used to be a
> $50 card. I doubt you'd get that much for it now, even though it has
> different art.

The values of these cards may well have changed due to the fortunes of
their associated games. Shadowfist was only recently resurrected and
Doomtown is out of print. Indeed, there are a number of variables
unaccounted for in the use of these cards as examples. Players may
simply change their minds about their relative value. Admittedly,
showing that reprints cause a change in value for their
previously-printed cognates is a difficult thing to show as it is a
positive statement and not a negative one, but it is necessary to
support it distinctly in order to prove that reprints harm the
secondary market. Plus, one must address why this decrease in value of
older cards doesn't universally happen. (Limited Edition Focus in L5R
has not decreased in value despite the fact that Focus was reprinted
in all the basic sets.) And then support must be given to show that
the fortunes of the secondary market directly affect the finances of
the parent company of the game in question. I do not believe such a
line of argument is correct.

-- Lemar Johnson

The term was more, from where I stood, being applied at Garou as a
whole, rather than the individualistic stance you take.

Because vampires have to drink blood, because vampires descend into the
Beast and so on, they can be considered *as a whole group* evil, by some
definitions.[0] The Garou, on the other hand, are less definably evil
in that general overall sense.

The point, however, was being made that it is difficult to define the
Garou as morally good, rather than specifically making them neutral.
The Gurahl war, the Get of Fenris and many other items provide
sufficient taint to make it hard to paint the Garou, as a whole, in a
good light.

Obviously, individuals differ from the stereotype, but the stereotype is
mostly what was being discussed. (IMO etc.)

[0] It is one of those difficult situations where creatures doing what
is natural to them is defined as evil. Tricky to handle.

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On 23 Jul 2001 16:21:01 -0700, Lemar Johnson wrote:

>Ih L5R and Rage feature relatively amoral societies. L5R features an

>entire underclass used as slave labor for their betters and casual
>death of subordinates for the pleasure of the ruling elite -- just
>like any feudal background.

I'm reminded of the sophisticated peasant who starts haranguing King
Arthur about his political system in Monty Python and the Holy Grail.
It's funny because it's so out of place.

What's equally incongruous is the way that players import their own
morality into VTES. See the current furore about the player who
actually threatened another. Or the way that many players insist that
keeping deals in an honourable manner is vital. The thing I liked
most about L5R were the little role-playing touches - the way you lost
honour if you backed up, "the table is yours", etc. These tried to
get you to play the game with a Japanese mind-set and it's a shame
that most players couldn't handle it.

Anyway, what this all goes to show is that Dancey was not some
unthinking puritan on a moral crusade. Did the remake of Rage change
its moral character in any way? Of his games, I know Doomtown best
and this contains a good mix of black hats, white hats and grey hats
like most westerns. There's plenty of immorality in there - one
faction even personifies the seven deadly sins. So what?

>Vampire presents us with a group of ancient vampires who manipulate
>other vampires. Though it's very likely that they or their pawns do
>bad things, there's nothing to suggest that what they do is anything
>near the scale of L5R. Jyhad is a very abstract game -- today's
>session could be about who gets control of Mexico or who gets control
>over this Rembrant painting I and Methuselah B over there have been
>arguing over for centuries. I'm not saying that vampires are good, but
>I am saying that trying to call one's role in the other card games out
>there "good" and the role one plays in VtES "bad" is an absurd thing.
>I must respectfully disagree with such a notion.

The relationship between players in Jyhad is one of "predator" and
"prey". The tone of the game is unremittingly dark and the
gothic/punk fin-de-siecle theme is pushed hard. It's not possible to
win the game in any other way than being nasty to your neighbours.
You can't take pride in the success of your clan because you don't
really have one - the minions are just unwitting puppets of an
anonymous Methusaleh.

Dancey saw these things as bad but they were not the reason for
declining to produce a new expansion:

>I reiterate again: VtES is not in active development because sales were
>insufficient to justify continued efforts for the brand, not due to my moral
>qualms.

Andrew

Perfect is the enemy of good. Great Britain and its former colony,
the USA, have made the world what it is today and all other countries
can't help but ape their successful culture (and language). The only
serious ideological opposition now comes from Red China - a
gerontocracy of crabby old men on the make - much like VTES's

Rage and Netrunner stayed dead in spite of what he did for them, not
because of it. In one case he revamped the game, in the other he just
produced more of the same. Neither was enough to revive them. If
he'd tackled VTES, I expect he'd have stayed away from a revamp - he
thought the game system was good. He didn't even want to introduce
radical new elements like Hunters and so that only leaves more of the

though. And there would probably have been more of a storyline.

18 million cards annually." Has WW reached this level?

game into a really big hit commercially. Critically, of course, nobody

sealed-deck two-player CCG there has ever been, but IMO the problem is

cyber suits, perhaps because a lot of us already ARE nerds and suits,
often simultaneously. i actually tried to rejig the NR mechanic to be
more DnD-ish, so the Runner was the adventurer and the Corporation was
the Dungeon-builder sorta thing. All just on 3x5 index cards, but it
was good fun, and i wrote to Jennifer Clarke Wilkes at WoTC about the

professionally. She replied that this had already been discussed, and
rejected on the grounds of not wanting to queer Magic's pitch.

the problem. i think doing it in such a way that all the old cards
became unusable WAS the problem. IMO, what was wrong with old rage was
that the timing was a terrible mess, cards kept drifting out of your
deck [because you used them to mark damage or long-lasting effects on
other minions/cards], and some of the cards were ridiculously
over-powered [Spirit Alias, anyone?]. Local playgroups had solved
these problems by using ad hoc timing rules, sleeves to keep track of
your own damage cards and card limits or bans for the real stinkers.

as i can tell, and this caused a great deal of unnecessary resentment
of and resistance to the new product.

forgotten. But you can't Rend someone's entrails in VTES nor can you

nonetheless.

Okay, now that all the petty crap about whether VTES is a CCG or not
is settled (I hope) we can get on to the meat of the problem.

"The Nosferatu Stuff" <roans...@yahoo.com> wrote:
> My worthless paper is this(as a limited example, please keep that in mind):

> far)
> Amria Common 19

> Fata Amria Rare 3
> Imposing Phantasm Rare 2
> Mirror Image Common 20
> Pseudo-Blindness Common 20
> Reality Common 23
> Red Herring Common 22
> Sensory Overload Common 19
> Shilmulo Deception Common 24

There's something I noticed when looking at this list and then looking
at the full list on the White Wolf web page. There are no "uncommon"
library cards. I'm uncertain whether this is a problem.

Personally, I don't have a problem with rare (and R1, formerly chase)
cards as it admittedly gives me a thrill when I get a hard to find
card that I've been trying to get multiples of. It's also a minor
frustration to be unable to build a deck concept because I don't have
enough of a given card, but it's the same thrill/frustration that I
get from video games...and I enjoy those, too.

However, the more I think about making some of the currently common
cards into "uncommon," I realize that they would compensate by making
common cards even more common, instead of making the rare cards less
rare. If they did both, esp. with the more utilitarian cards, you'd
probably have a better mix.

Of course, that's just my opinion, I could be wrong.

Regards,
Noal

Messages.Author: Lemar Johnson

James Coupe <ja...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote in message news:<xm6cUtDV...@gratiano.zephyr.org.uk>...

> In message <5219faff.01072...@posting.google.com>, Lemar
> Johnson <vay...@hotmail.com> writes

> >

> >Everything in HoR was Unique, by necessity.
>
> Hmm... this makes me think that this sort of high-powered (appropriately
> costed, of course), action-packed sort of set is unlikely to work in the
> No Limits world of V:TES, as a result, whereas it could work happily in
> any number of other card games.

It is ironic that you should say this. As a matter of fact, the cards
in HoR were actually very weak! Most of them were vastly overcosted
powerhouses. Something you must understand about L5R if you don't play
it is that permanents aren't too permanent -- if you spend all your
resources on a monster, rest assured that his time is short.

Of course, this happens in Jyhad to a lesser degree. But L5R is
particularly brutal.

But I digress. In any event, only two or three of those cards were
truly flexible or strong, and one of the best of those was faction
specific (Naga -- who'd of thought they'd get the most efficient
Personality in the set?). The one card that was really, truly strong
-- Judgement -- can only be used in a very narrow deck archetype.
(Dishonor Duelling.) And THAT card should have been availible in
boosters because of its important place in the story.

Like I said, not a happy set. :-)

Again, if the cards in HoR had been extremely strong, players would
have become very, very mad. "Let's see, you get three copies of a
non-Unique game-breaker from a set I didn't know existed that costs
$80 minimum and use them against me in tourney..."'

As to your point, yes, if Jyhad had sets they would need to be vanilla
and basic to have a good effect. Lots of cards you'd build a deck
around, but no overpowered obscenities. Much like how starters are
done now, to branch off towards another contention mentioned on this
thread.

> (Of course, I note the points about being unhappy about excluding
> players, cost and so forth. I'm thinking merely more in terms of
> mechanics and game impact.)

Point taken. The newness of the card game phenomenon for hobby games
doesn't give us all a wealth of examples to debate from, so I expect
all our analogies will leave much to be desired.

-- Lemar Johnson

Oh, he's not. The World of Darkness games are not about going abroud
and facing evil in some hellhole at the edge of the Earth. The WoD
games are about going down to the convenience store to get some cough
drops and finding EVIL, there, in the aisle, behind the counter, and
in the foundations of the building itself. Then you go home -- more
evil!

To speak more clearly: every faction -- *every* faction -- in the WoD
does bad things. (Except the Salubri. But if you don't know what
Salout is responsible for, I won't tell you...) Legbiter just
scratches the surface here. Think about it this way: without metahuman
abilities, what are political organizations in the Real World
responsible for historically and in the present day. In the U.S., the
Democrats were considered, for the latter half of the century, to be
the "party of the people" <snickering removed>. But guess which party,
Democrats or Republicans, was frothingly pro-slavery in the 1800s? And
the Republicans of yesteryear weren't anti-slavery because they read
their Bibles closely and realized the evils of placing men in bondage,
but they feared for jobs for poorer whites (slave labor being, in
essesnce, free). And that's a century of history off. White Wolf
critters hang around for milennia.

And, in the present day, they still do bad stuff. A WoD character with
a good heart will spend most of his time slapping down the peers of
his faction -- an Order of Hermes mage of good intentions will
revitalize the selfish and hidebound practices of his order, a
Toreador of fine repute will police his own clan for excess, and a
Shadow Lord on the straight and narrow will infight with the best of
'em -- but if he finds a tribe-brother who has a single strand of fur
out of place he'll take him down.

> Ahah, well that is probably our major point of difference. My werewolf
> name is Rends-the-Treehuggers, my auspice is Ahroun [really!] and my
> tribe is the Black Spiral Dancers. i used to be a treehugger in RL,
> but i got badly turned off by what i see as the Fascistic trends in
> Green thought. And before i was a treehugger i was a trotskyite, and i
> left THAT sect over what i saw as ignorant workerism over the Ulster
> Workers Strike. Nowadays i'm in the curious political position of
> being a socialist and an eco-politico whilst COMPLETELY unable to
> support any Green or left-of-labour party.

The natural result of thought-out political convictions will
eventually be the rejection of all large political parties that one
does not have firm influence in. This is because large parties do not
exist to serve oneself or one's interest first, but to perpetuate
themselves. When given options between perpetuating themselves and
bending themselves more closely to the will of the people of a nation,
they must choose the former. I wouldn't be surprised if the next wave
of voting practices in western natures features people voting
completly based on the candidate, disregarding the party supporting
the candidate as a secondary factor at best.

And with that, we move way the hell off topic. Getting back...

> He did a good job on Lo5R, for sure.

Not all L5R players share this opinion. It's a relative thing and a
long story, so we'll leave it at that.

>And they DID bring out new cards
> for Netrunner and a new version of Rage. i think the NR Classic
> expansion was really very good, and i find it sad that so few people
> appreciate that very, VERY fine game.

I didn't know there was another NetRunner expansion. Or maybe I did
and I'm confusing it -- there was only one expansion, yes?

> > I think his point was that having such games in your portfolio was bad
> > for the company's image and so bad for business (i.e. would hurt
> > sales).
>
> Here is the bit where you seem to be agreeing with the rest of us that
> Dancey DID find VTES repugnant.

This is odd, too -- whilst there have been groups angry about Magic
because it has sorcerous connotations, Jyhad never had any criticism.
(I never tire of this irony: parent groups will leap on a game or
hobby that seems to incidentally resemble an ancient religious
prohibition, but they will ignore those pasttimes which feature
violence as a means of achieving goals, despite most modern faith's
condemnations of such. Poekemon's cockfighting was embraced by parents
but Magic gets slammed for spellcasting.) Dancey's paranoia about
Jyhad's image reflection seems irrational, at best.

> >
> > Some folk suggested that a Hunter/Slayer expansion would be a good way
> > of addressing this but he didn't go for it - said that he expected
> > that existing fans would be hostile. It's a shame he didn't give this
> > a try as I would probably have liked it.
>
> i would like to see this, too, and so would Sarah i'm sure. i know it
> sounds funny but we really, REALLY don't like vampires.

What's to like? They're immortal monsters who need to be destroyed for
the sake of humanity. Some of the clans are neat, though, in concept.
Hunter, on the other hand, sucked, and sucked bigtime. I abhor it. It
completly contradicted the only cool thing about fighting vampires: a
mortal had to be constantly on his toes because his foes are holding
most of the cards. Instead, Hunter first made these people metahumans,
in complete defiance to established theme and common sense, then
categorized them in typical, deplorable White Wolf fashion. Everything
they touch must have clans. Hunter is a piece of crap. If humans are
to have a bigger role in Jyhad, especially as opposition to Kindred
activities, the designers would be well advised to seek inspiration
from other sources than their parent company.

> Was the Wyrm expansion for
> > Rage a success? Did players like playing the opposition?
>
> Opinions differ about that. Most of the Rage players i know LOVED it
> but as another poster remarks further down this was not a universal
> feeling. Not controversial is that the Wyrm had the best foil in Count
> Vladimir Rustovich and the worst foil in Churjoroc's tusk.

Not controversial? Then why did you bring it up? Did you mean that it
was not _un_controversial?

> feeling. Not controversial is that the Wyrm had the best foil in Count
> Vladimir Rustovich and the worst foil in Churjoroc's tusk.

Oh, how I loved Churjoc's Tusk! It represented almost everything that
was wrong with Rage! For those not in the know:

The Tusk is an ultra-rare foil card. It allows you to kill off the
powerful Black Spiral Dancer character that holds it (it has a high
Gnosis requirement, meaning the holder is probably significant). So
you're down a peep -- a good one. But wait, there's more. You can go
through your deck and grab a Nexus Crawler, the most powerful Enemy in
the game, to join your pack -- for three turns, after which he goes
away, too. So it's a minor gain, net.

But wait, the Nexus Crawler is a rare card thats obscenely hard to
get. From a previous set.

And, though the Nexus Crawler is fearsome, many basic commons
(Nightmare Coin, etc.) allowed you to escape him.

This was hilarious, IMO.

> Noal McDonald <dhar...@none-of-your-fscking-business.com> wrote:
> The terms used contradict since, within the industry, the terms
> themselves are used casually and interchangeably.

How does the interchangeability and casualty of two terms' usage
establish a contradiction?

> We do not use them casually, here, because they would make this
> thread even more ambiguous.

Would you care to support that satement?

I made that statement that VTES is a collectable card game. My
statement is supporeted by the facts that WotC and WW both have
marketed VTES as "collectable" and there are collectors that acquire
VTES cards only to complete a set, rather than play the game. It is
advertised as being collectable and people collect it, therefore it is
a CCG.

In addition, People trade to complete collections or deck desings and
it is marketed as tradeable, therefore it is a TCG.

Therefore, my original statement that VTES is both a CCG and a CCG is
correct.

How is that ambiguous in any way? More importantly, how does not
taking into consideration all aspects of a product's usage and
marketing further obscure this thread, except to refute claims made by
those on one side of the issue?

> The issue at hand was whether or not White Wolf markets
> VtES game components as collectible pieces, primarily, or whether the
> emphasis on was their use as game components.

No, the issue was whether White Wolf could ignore the importance of
the collectability of VTES in the secondary market and the impact it
has on the profitability of the product. Clearly, the game design
itself has an emphasis on the game function, the distribution of cards
in booster packs has an emphasis on establishing its collectability
and marketing attempts to balance both goals. Again, there is no
ambiguity.

> (And note that this was a minor issue indeed in my previous post;

From your post:

> No WoTC TCG is marketed as a CG.

> In addition, as we have already mentioned, VtES is not marketed as
> presenting a collectable set.

> Um, again, VtES isn't marked as collectable, ever.

Minor, my ass. Why is it that when somebody makes a statement
repeatedly and then it is refuted, they write it off as "minor"?

> I have not seen White Wolf cater specifically to collectors in any concise,
> meaningful way since their acquisition of VtES;

Their repeated use of the word "collectable" in multiple places,
including a press release, suggests that they aren't ignoring
collectors either.

> I have not seen significant on-line support from the parent company for
> VtES collection by collectors,

That is because, by fair use laws, companies are normally prohibited
from influencing the cost of copyrighted products in the secondary
market. However, EULA contracts, such as that on software and concert
tickets, usually take precendence. In this instance, VTES has no such
EULA so normal laws apply.

> I was not arrogant in my post; it seems you have done your best to
> paint me as such so you yourself could come off as arrogant.
> And no, I was not arrogant in this post, either. I was disparaging.

dis·par·age (di-sparij) tr.v. 1.To speak of in a slighting or
disrespectful way; belittle.

Explain to me the practical difference between being arrogant and
being belittling?

Translation: You were being a fuck nut and when I ran rough shod over
you for it, you cried foul. Cry a river all you like, jackass. I don't
give a fuck. You got what you deserved.

> My advice: find something, outside of these postings, to take pride in.
> If your ego is too fragile to handle disagreement,

That advice, like all the rest of your statements thus far, is worth
the paper it's printed on. My ego is far from fragile and I can not
only handle constructive, informed disagreement, I revel in it. When
you can provide such, I'll be happy to debate it on its merits.

Which brings me to this:

> Next time you post, please have enough self-respect to spell-check
> your shoddy work. An "argument," indeed.

The last gasp of a person who is losing an argument, and desperately
wants to win at all costs, is almost always a flame about misspellings

instead of coming off as an intelligent, yet condescending, disputant,
they come off as an obnoxious ass clown. For future reference, "spell
check" is not a hyphenated word.

credibility.
