Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 23 Jul 2001 16:37:56 GMT, Robert Goudie wrote:

>I don't have a problem with a company wanting high moral standards. But you're
>a fool if you think Ryan was just parroting a specific standard from Peter
>Adkison. Don't you think its a bit unlikely that the same individuals who
>created the game would find the game offensive?

Not in the case of Peter Adkison - he stated that his girlfriend had
raised his consciousness. But it's clear that Ryan thought that VTES
had a unsavoury backstory. The issue is whether this determined his
policy. Digging back even further, I find the following quote from
you in Jan 98:

>It is my understanding that Ryan Dancey (the VTES Brand Manager at FRPG)
>was instrumental in getting The Sabbat re-released this past October.
>This reprint is somewhat of a test for VTES. No products in '98 isn't
>the end of the world. We have a whole year to increase interest with
>demos and tournaments. I'm going to wait for the '99 catalogue before
>I panic.

It appears that the first thing Ryan did when becoming responsible for
the game in Oct 97 was to arrange for the Sabbat reprint. This is the
most repellent VTES set - the Sabbat's morality is clear and the art
reflects this. But Dancey printed it anyway. Presumably it failed
the implicit sales test but you didn't wait for the '99 catalogue and
started panicking in Feb 98.

It's also interesting to see his similar comments on Netrunner in Feb
98. This appears to be the same situation as VTES. He lists various
flaws with the game. You could take issue with any or all of these -
the lack of good/bad duality was supposed to be a flaw of VTES. But
the bottom line was that the game just wasn't selling - that's what
really mattered.

Andrew

>NR-L: Netrunner fans are obviously disappointed by WotC's
>choice to put the game "on maintenance." What is it that
>keeps it there?

>RD: To be blunt: lack of sales. If I thought that
>Netrunner could generate enough interest to maintain a
>limited production schedule, I'd print it. We're currently
>putting some ideas into place to gauge what the actual
>market interest is for the game, and if results are
>favorable, we'll reopen a discussion on printing more cards.

>NR-L: Does Netrunner have some insurmountable tragic flaw?

>RD: Netrunner has four major issues it must overcome, which
>I will simply list instead of getting into a whole lot of
>gory detail:

>1. Lack of "Tribalization." There are no factional alliances
>for the players.

>2. Good Guy/Bad Guy duality. It's tough to play the runner
>and the corp instead of one or the other.

>3. No value from license. The R. Talsorian license doesn't
>contribute much to the game.

>4. No concept of "you." It is difficult to relate to a game
>where "you" are an abstracted participant.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <20363D0D1A6C4CEC.C01787D7...@lp.airnew
s.net>, Andrew S. Davidson <a...@csi.com> writes

>The game would be better in this
>respect if each player had a permanent master card like the outfit
>homes in Doomtown, the clan strongholds in L5R or the Vanguard cards
>in Magic. Is there background to drawn on here - are the Methusalehs
>named and characterised in the WoD books?

Such has been suggested and debated a number of times, not least in
Darkness Unveiled where Methuselah archetypes were suggested.

There is a lot of difficult grafting these onto the game, however, in a
way that is balanced now. That something like Lo5R was drawn up with
the strongholds early on makes it easier to fiddle with them.

Also, it is difficult to add them into the game given the balance that
has been gained between one tricky ponies and toolbox decks, and they're
always difficult to add anyway.

Consider say:

Big Bashy Methuselah
Put this card in play at the start of the game. Tap this card and pay 1
pool to give your minions +1 hand damage until your next untap phase.
Whilst this card is tapped, you cannot play reaction cards.

The down-side is pointless, because you simply construct a (perfectly
viable) deck to avoid it, if you're someone like Peter playing a weenie
Brujah rush deck.

The toolbox deck, however, would be significantly affected by it, such
that it would be difficult to find one that worked without seriously
killing you.

Don't listen to him, Leggy. The "metahuman" angle of Hunter
is only there to keep your characters from becoming grease spots
on the front wheel of a vampire's Hawg or from having your
Entrails Rended too easily. The important part of the game (if you

Actually, I quite like bits of Hunter. (Not played it, however.)

Addressing the clan point first of all, well, yes, it's a big White Wolf
thing. But it actually *works* on a story-telling (and a Story-Telling)
level. If you treat everyone as individuals, completely free to do what
they want, however they want, it tends to be less easy to make
significant impact with them. If you set up stereotypes and systems and
deviate within those constraints, you can get a lot more fulfilment and
satisfaction out of the end result. (Whilst it's not the only way for
art to work, by any means, it's the way quite a large amount of good art
(literature, music, painting etc.) works.)

A person who fights against the vileness of the Tzimisce clan, grappling
a few last vestiges of humanity, living on their wits, hiding from what
they've become, can have a far more significant, dramatic impact.
Treating everyone as individuals within a framework of stereotypes is
good, IMO.

On Hunter specifically, there are some nice elements. First of all,
it's the first major RPG from White Wolf I've seen where the players
don't have a clue what's going on. A rogue Caitiff in V:tM or a self-
aware Orphan in Mage are about the closest you get. Much of Hunter can
be driven as personal exploration, a character trying to figure out who
and what they are in context, without a friendly Sire or Tribe to
educate them. Those who have anyone to talk to should usually be far
more rare than those who don't.

The system is also quite loose, in that there are only three basic
"clans", providing structure without the temptation of rigid shackles.

The game is also very *now*, in a manner that WtA gets close to.
Vampire has a lot of gothic history playing behind it, and it's all too
easy to view the here and now as just as extension of all that's gone
on. Mage and Wraith can get tied up in their own self, rather than
interacting with the world, if they're not careful. Changeling is Just
Plain Odd. Hunter is here, Hunter is now, with seat-of-the-pants
technology. It's a very immediate game. There isn't the Jyhad guiding
your actions. You don't feel that everything is necessarily going to
end up in Apocalypse despite what you do. The problems are *right
there* in front of you. What you do will, of course, have an effect on
the long term future, but it will also affect things Right Now.

There are some down-sides, mostly mechanical. Ward is ludicrously
powerful. A character with a couple of points will be able to hold you
at bay relatively easily. They're rolling Stamina+Zeal, you're rolling
Stamina. You have to beat their number of successes! And the power
lasts for the entire scene without concentration.

For me, one of the really nice things about Hunter is that you can
imagine almost anyone becoming Imbued. It could, quite literally, be
you that goes out and sees the Walking Dead and hears the call.[0] With
Ward, I can't do jack about you unless I have good ranged weapon skills
- a gun, or throwing knives. How many 'ordinary' people are any good
with such? Imagine your wife, your boss, your mother, your postman.
Any of those could be Imbued. Unlike Vampire, there isn't the
likelihood of someone screening you for ages. Unlike Mage, you aren't
likely to be particularly self-aware/intelligent (in that sort of
sense). Werewolf has the whole parentage thing - you have inherited the
traits of another Werewolf, so you should hopefully be vaguely cut out
for it. That a few cock-ups like this mean that, if someone starts
using these powers extensively, you would have to min-max to get by them
(creating powerful stats sheets, rather than interesting characters) is
moderately annoying.

[0] Metaphorically speaking, in a literal sense. Or something.



The concept was small monthly releases - 50 card sets packed as
commons and uncommons with a couple of fixed unique cards in the
starter. By buying a starter and 8 boosters, a player would get all
the cards he needed for that month. That would cost about $25 - a
comparatively painless amount compared the cost of a set in the
traditional model. The idea was to get players to place a regular
standing order in the same way that they bought every issue of their
favorite comics.

I think it mainly didn't work because a player wouldn't want to buy a
whole box unless he could split it with someone and you needed about 8
players to soak up a big combo box. If the retail order unit had been
smaller, it might have worked better.

Andrew

I do maybe 10% of my trading with my local group, maybe less. I've
completed some 20 or so online trades since "catching the bug," and haven't
been burned yet. It's not like I'm out there in a high-demand forum
attracting predatory frauders. Also, there are some excellent sites

>
>Yes, unlike everyone else on this list, >I< know exactly what I'm
>talking about when it comes to VtES/Jyhad. Unlike >you< I have seen
>the financials, the P&L, the contracts, the cost of goods, the
>business plan, the expenses in marketing, the organized play figures,
>and every other scrap of detail regarding the brand.
>
>TCGs die. That's an observable fact. The reasons why they die are
>legion, but there is one underlying reason that each and every dead
>TCG has passed away:
>
>LACK OF SALES.
>
>I just don't know how to put it in any plainer terms. VtES >DOESN"T
>SELL< It sells in dribs and drabs and bits and peices, and in some
>places it sells really, really well. Those places are an anomoly, and
>there are not enough of them to justify printing new cards. And
>what's worse, VtES, unlike a whole lot of other games, has an
>international base of players, so sales can come globally, not just
>domestically - AND IT STILL DOESN'T SELL ENOUGH CARDS.
>
>Sales for every printing of Jyhad/VtES product were vastly smaller
>than projected. The final product, The Sabbat, even though it was
>printed in two batches, was had a huge card count, and had the most
>consumer-unfriendly distribution packout in the entire industry
>>barely< broke even, and if all costs were fully and accurately
>loaded, it would have lost tens of thousands of dollars. Products at
>FRPG >always< have full and accurate cost loads - when I say something
>makes money, it makes money. When I say something loses money, it
>loses money - no cheap accounting tricks to shift dollars around.
>
>See, with a trading card game, you can't print a couple of hundred
>thousand cards. You've got to print at least six million cards,
>minimum, in order to break even on all the costs associated with
>supporting a TCG brand. Six million cards works out to be about
>10,000 displays of product (15 card boosters, 36 boosters per
>display). In order to sell 10,000 displays of product, every actively
>purchasing adventure game store in the US would have to purchase >FOUR
>DISPLAYS OF PRODUCT<. That's an unreasonable amount to expect to sell
>sucessfully. What's worse, on average, only 30% of the domestic AGI
>stores buy any TCG other than Magic, Star Wars or L5R with any
>regularity. If only 30% of them bought those displays, they'd each
>need to buy twelve units - an impossibility.
>
>Another VtES problem: I can't put it into Rolling Thunder. If the
>initial sales of the product tank, I'm stuck with 2/3 of the print run
>and absolutely no way to sell it. With a risky proposition like a
>VtES expansion, to protect myself and the company, I've got to ship
>those six million cards out the door on release day. We couldn't RT
>the game until we were certain that we'd sell at least three
>consecutive months of product.
>
>The overseas market for non Magic, non media-licensend TCGs is about
>25% the size of the domestic market. For VtES, the European market
>offers some hope, as they tended to buy VtES product in higher ratios
>than other similar products, but even there, the purchase potential is
>vastly smaller than that necessary to make the brand viable.
>
>I could go into a long diatribe on the current condition of the market
>(the channel is >really< messed up, even though many of the retailers
>are healthy and the consumer base remains enthusiastic), but I won't,
>not only because it's a depressing speech, but it is somewhat
>proprietary information. I will say that sales on TCGs across the
>board are down, that the distributors are unwilling to take any
>inventory risk (thus, there is no sales potential) for anything but
>the most viable TCG brands, and that the immense amount of unsold
>Jyhad/VtES product clogging the channel is a nearly unscalable barrier
>to entry for a new VtES release. Even if we printed it, it's
>debatable wether we could get anyone to stock it at distribution, or
>anyone to order it at retail.
>
>If all of those issues were addressed, and we had a strong business
>case to invest in further VtES work, then there are several second
>order issues involving the product that would need to be addressed
>internally, not only within FRPG, but within WotC as well before we
>moved ahead with that development. In the great scheme of things, I
>only have so many dollars, and so many people to allocate to
>developing products, and I have to choose those brands that I believe
>have the highest percentage chance of returning the most money on that
>investment possible. VtES faces >substantial< challenges in that
>department as well.
>
>As always when I discuss VtES, I must stress that I found the game to
>be well designed and executed, and that the underlying license from
>White Wolf is one of the most well concieved and executed licenses in
>the gaming industry.
>
>
>Ryan S. Dancey
>Brand Manager, Five Rings Publishing Group
>Wizards of the Coast

vote is for a Hunter expansion!

"Gomi no Sensei" <go...@best.com> wrote

>

> like Kiasyd and Ahrimanes, but does not include Serpents of the Light,
> at least as far as I'm aware. Bah.

Ahrimanes are still 'canon' so to speak but have all gone missing within the
World of Darkness 'meta-story'. No explanation has been given why to the
best of my knowledge.

The Kiasyd are definitely still an active V:tM bloodline, but like the
Harbingers of Skulls, True Brujah and Blood Brothers, they are recommended
to be played only as NPCs by Storytellers. They're fairly disruptive when
played as PCs, though an all-Blood Brother coterie strikes me as pretty
neat.

The Baali are an active, antagonistic bloodline in the Dark Ages but
supposedly extinct in modern V:tM (yeah, right). Show me an ST that hasn't
used Baali in the modern day and I'll show you an ST that hasn't run out of
ideas :)

Gargoyles, Salubri, Samedi and Daughters of Cacophany are all active, known
to exist but are still fairly uncommon.

All of the 'bloodlines' are rare enough that most modern vampires would
probably never have heard of them.

And yeah, having some Serpents of the Light and more Ravnos Antritribu might
be a good idea. The Ventrue Antitribu have been changed back to the regular
clan disciplines, so that combination can be explored (actually has already
if you've noticed the !Ven made *since* the Sabbat expansion). Malkavians
could be given DEM. More City Gangrel could be made. A few 'Black Hand'
Assamite Antitribu might be welcome... There are a lot of options for future
expansions really... enough that I'm surprised Bloodlines was chosen before
other ideas.

Cheers,
WES

FRPG -- Five Rings Publishing Group -- was L5R's original home (a
collaboration between Alderac and damn-I-forget). The execution of
L5R's design has caused their initial fan-based to become alienated in
the last few years. Basically, the basic problems of design the game
has have mostly gotten worse instead of improving, though there was
vast room for the design to take a different direction. An example:
this is a 3 CL game; when you make, in a later-day expansion, three
more cards that do the same basic thing as the basic set version of a
powerful card, you've strengthened the deck archetypes that were based
around that card immesurably. We've seem some archetypes grow stronger
since they heyday of Imperial Edition (the first set) while others
have languished. For several years. Despite player support.

And that's without details for brevity's sake. Plus, I rant enough as
it is.

Messages.Body:
Andrew S. Davidson <a...@csi.com> wrote in message news:<57D486D29D634398.BFF53697...@lp.airnews.net>...
> On Wed, 25 Jul 2001 00:34:05 -0400, Wes wrote:
>
> >I always hate coming across as the ignorant one, but what the hell is
> >Rolling Thunder? I thought you were referring to a game at first, but it
> >sounds more like a distribution concept of some kind?

<snip>

> I think it mainly didn't work because a player wouldn't want to buy a
> whole box unless he could split it with someone and you needed about 8
> players to soak up a big combo box. If the retail order unit had been
> smaller, it might have worked better.
>
> Andrew

Actually, the Powers That Be submitted a post that said one of its
major problems was in distributing: the stores had no idea what to
order. Thus, they ordered lots and lots of the first Scroll or edition
of a given game, but didn't realize that the next Scrolls or editions
were different products. This resulted in a glut of the earlier
product and a shortage of the later, which led to huge amounts of
cards sitting on shelves -- which stores hate. Things rolled downhill
from there. (E.g., other bad things happen I don't remember clearly
enough to explain without digging up old references.)

I do know that my experience with it was actually good. The small sets
did allow me, as a player who budgeted little cash for games, to get
the cards I wanted.

-- Lemar Johnson

dhar...@my-deja.com (Noal McDonald) wrote in message news:<bb705c59.0107...@posting.google.com>...
> > Noal McDonald <dhar...@none-of-your-fscking-business.com> wrote:
> > The terms used contradict since, within the industry, the terms
> > themselves are used casually and interchangeably.
>
> How does the interchangeability and casualty of two terms' usage
> establish a contradiction?

Only within the context of some of the posts in this thread which
imply that the use of collectable and trading would suggest different
marketing procedures, procedures which many people thought significant
to their arguments here. The differences (that these procedures would
or could create) to the Powers That Be may or may not be negligible,
but it is a point of contention for those in this forum. Whether it's
a terribly significant point of contention remains to be seen, but
people on the net (us) will debate for debating's sake, so it doesn't
matter much.

> > We do not use them casually, here, because they would make this
> > thread even more ambiguous.
>
> Would you care to support that satement?

There was no support needed for the satement. None needed for the
statement, either. It wasn't a contention, but an observation. If we
(within this thread) used them casually (interchangeably, as the full
text of my previous post described) we would become confused.

> I made that statement that VTES is a collectable card game. My
> statement is supporeted by the facts that WotC and WW both have
> marketed VTES as "collectable" and there are collectors that acquire
> VTES cards only to complete a set, rather than play the game. It is
> advertised as being collectable and people collect it, therefore it is
> a CCG.

It is not supported as a primarily collectable item. Where are the
carrying cases and ultra-rares? To forgo what's been said before,
White Wolf indicates that it believes the health of the IP is directly
and most strongly linked to the playability of the game itself and
very much less so to its ability to be hoarded into sets. We thus
treat it as a game that can be collected.

> In addition, People trade to complete collections or deck desings and
> it is marketed as tradeable, therefore it is a TCG.
>
> Therefore, my original statement that VTES is both a CCG and a CCG is
> correct.

> How is that ambiguous in any way?

Well, for one you used "CCG" twice above.

You misunderstood me. I did not say you were being ambiguous, or
anyone else in the thread. I said WotC and WW's use of the terms were
ambiguous and, for them, functionally interchangeable -- at least, for
WW (WotC may have issues with it). The context of my reply when I used
the term ambiguous was that of the parent companies' usage of the
term.

> More importantly, how does not
> taking into consideration all aspects of a product's usage and
> marketing further obscure this thread, except to refute claims made by
> those on one side of the issue?

This argument stems from the misunderstanding described above, which
is unfortunate, because cutely-loaded arguments are fun to meet.

> > The issue at hand was whether or not White Wolf markets
> > VtES game components as collectible pieces, primarily, or whether the
> > emphasis on was their use as game components.
>
> No, the issue was whether White Wolf could ignore the importance of
> the collectability of VTES in the secondary market and the impact it
> has on the profitability of the product.

Nope, I was right the first time. Note that I originally discussed the
utility and gain from printing fixed sets of cards for Jyhad. The only
reason I entered the discussion was because the very hypothetical
possibility was bandied about. I believe such printings would add to
the quality of the game. The primary emphasis of VtES as a collector's
item or a game is thus a significant issue to me -- and was a point in
my earlier post. If VtES is a game, first, then its success would be
linked to its success as a game. I then sought to show that the
existence of sets does not necessarily undermine the value of boosters
or harm the secondary market (and other posts from people from various
sides of the issue have pointed out that the secondary market's
fortunes do not directly benefit the parent company of the game, if at
all).

At no point did I suggest WW "ignore the importance of the
collectability of VtES" or challenge its collectability. In fact, I
pointed out that the creation of boxed sets with cards in formats
varying from the mixed boosters preserves the collectability of the
original, random set. Thus, whether or not WW markets VtES as a
collectable card game or not is less significant to me than any of
these other issues as I have no doubt that the fortunes of this game
depend upon its appreciation as a game -- and have no doubt WW
believes the same. I find that WW concentrates upon the play-aspect of
Jyhad more than any other aspect within its design, thus leading me to
believe that they market it as a game first. But even if I was wrong,
the contention that Jyhad's fortune is based on its enjoyment when
played is strong contention as far as I'm concerned, making it a moot
issue: if Jyhad stops being fun to play, the product dies. If WW has
been marketing this game as a collector's item primarily and has been
inexplicably generous with the game-aspect of it up to this point but
then, at some future time, places its emphasis back to its collectable
aspect rather than upon play, they will kill their sales.

(And because I do believe WW to be a bit more attentive to profit than
that, I hold that they do, indeed, consider this a game first.)

>Clearly, the game design
> itself has an emphasis on the game function, the distribution of cards
> in booster packs has an emphasis on establishing its collectability
> and marketing attempts to balance both goals. Again, there is no
> ambiguity.

Again, this line of thought is corrected above.

> > (And note that this was a minor issue indeed in my previous post;
>
> From your post:
>
> > No WoTC TCG is marketed as a CCG.

> > In addition, as we have already mentioned, VtES is not marketed as
> > presenting a collectable set.
>
> > Um, again, VtES isn't marked as collectable, ever.
>
> Minor, my ass. Why is it that when somebody makes a statement
> repeatedly and then it is refuted, they write it off as "minor"?

Why is it that when someone has their statements refuted they turn to
cursing?

The argument pertaining to the marketing of Jyhad, as described above,
is, again, ancillary to the argument pertaining to the benefit of
printing sets. It is, indeed, minor; the argument about the viability
of constructed sets does not depend upon the contention pertaining to
VtES being first a collection or a game, but the argument about sets
is supported by the contention that VtES is a game first.

> > I have not seen White Wolf cater specifically to collectors in any concise,
> > meaningful way since their acquisition of VtES;
>
> Their repeated use of the word "collectable" in multiple places,
> including a press release, suggests that they aren't ignoring
> collectors either.

The above statement does not contradict my argument. The use of the
phrase has been already described as a convenience. I was discussing
whether or not the game had its collectability emphasized or its
play-value emphasized.

> > I have not seen significant on-line support from the parent company for
> > VtES collection by collectors,
>
> That is because, by fair use laws, companies are normally prohibited
> from influencing the cost of copyrighted products in the secondary
> market. However, EULA contracts, such as that on software and concert
> tickets, usually take precendence. In this instance, VTES has no such
> EULA so normal laws apply.

This would not prohibit the parent company from providing checklists
within starters, selling card-books, etc. -- other spin-offs that
collectors could find use for. I did not describe market manipulation
-- you argue against a contention I never made. Put simply, I find
that the absence of literature on the net and within VtES products to
encourage the collection of sets (instead of encouraging play -- there
is plenty of the latter) does not support the idea that VtES is
primarily marketed as a collectable set of pieces.

> > I was not arrogant in my post; it seems you have done your best to
> > paint me as such so you yourself could come off as arrogant.
> > And no, I was not arrogant in this post, either. I was disparaging.
>
> dis·par·age (di-sparij) tr.v. 1.To speak of in a slighting or
> disrespectful way; belittle.
>
> Explain to me the practical difference between being arrogant and
> being belittling?

Ah. You have taken it upon yourself to selectively delete portions of
my post which would undermine your rant. Do not worry -- it is a
common accident. I will reprint what I originally wrote to add clarity
to the following discussion:

"And no, I was not arrogant in this post, either. I was disparaging. I
do not think myself better than the person who responded, but I did
find his attitude leaving much to be desired (though I am certain that
he is, in fact, a decent human being of course). I specifically picked
nits in what I found to be a rant by a person who was acting out in a
verbally-abusive manner. I would much rather have my person attacked
after I have transgressed. As the order has been upturned, I thought
it best to rectify the situation by transgressing now."

As I said before, I found the attitude to leave much to be desired.
Thus, I acted in a disparaging way towards the substance of the post
and towards the temperament it suggested, which I feel I was well
within my rights to do -- the originator had attacked me verbally,
without provocation, and I responded in kind, but went no further.

To be sure of the issue, let us parallel the actions of our peer here
and define arrogant:

(ar'u-gunt), —adj.
1. making claims or pretensions to superior importance or rights;
overbearingly assuming; insolently proud: an arrogant public official.
2. characterized by or proceeding from arrogance: arrogant claims.

As my claims are well-founded and I do not claim, in any way, to be of
higher status than the one who attacked me in the first place, I am
indeed free from this label. In addition, it is more than possible,
from the definition given by the one I reply to here, to be
disparaging of an institution, an e-mail, or even a verbal stance or
attitude. None of this requires one to be disparaging of one or more
individuals associated with such.

> Translation: You were being a fuck nut and when I ran rough shod over
> you for it, you cried foul. Cry a river all you like, jackass. I don't
> give a fuck. You got what you deserved.

Again, you misrepresent me -- but at least we are being consistent. I
did not cry foul, though I did point out your arguments lacked merit
(which may well be the source of this resentment that causes you to
curse -- but that is supposition).

And if you didn't "give a fuck", why have you read thus far in this
and other posts which not only disagree with you but question the
character you display upon the net? Your continued attendance to this
lists betrays concern.

As to the supposition that I was "being a fuck nut," note that I
claimed all along that you began the attacks (with selective editing
and hostile comments). This would suggest you sought to instigate an
issue. If you thought I was "being a fuck nut," and were honestly
distressed by it, it would have behooved you to point out where I
insulted you such that your following insults and defamations would be
somewhat justified. The lack of such revelations does not seem to
suggest an oversight on your part but a lack of righteous basis --
that is, you did not seek to suggest exactly why you were in the right
because you are clearly in the wrong. This is supposition -- you
could, indeed, have simply missed said opportunity. But, still, you
make no attempt to show that you are not, indeed, "being a fuck nut."
Whatever you want that to mean.

> > My advice: find something, outside of these postings, to take pride in.
> > If your ego is too fragile to handle disagreement,
>
> That advice, like all the rest of your statements thus far, is worth
> the paper it's printed on. My ego is far from fragile and I can not
> only handle constructive, informed disagreement, I revel in it. When
> you can provide such, I'll be happy to debate it on its merits.

I have, and you haven't -- but this won't get us very far, I know, as
I have already seen you disparage the arguments and persons of others
besides myself in this thread without responding in a constructive
manner -- when they themselves were constructive.

> Which brings me to this:
>
> > Next time you post, please have enough self-respect to spell-check
> > your shoddy work. An "argument," indeed.
>
> The last gasp of a person who is losing an argument, and desperately
> wants to win at all costs, is almost always a flame about misspellings
> and typos.

Ah, Jason replied here accurately. And do note: I explained my
nitpicks clearly, and they had nothing to do with the arguments, but
with the attack upon my person. Selective editing once again.

And, if we accomplish nothing else, I am very proud of the fact that
you now spell "argument" correctly. Though there may be bitterness in
you, I know that we have made a step forward in one aspect.

>I find it amusing that when people do so, they invariably
> misspell something as well. The reason I find it amusing is that,
> instead of coming off as an intelligent, yet condescending, disputant,
> they come off as an obnoxious ass clown.

Did you mean to use the term "ass clown" as one phrase? I've never
heard of one, though it does give rise to a mental image that is a
little amusing but extremely unhygenic. I think you originally
intended for "ass" to be a modifier of "obnoxious", requiring a hyphen
as shown:

"obnoxious-ass clown"

This seems to reach your meaning more clearly.

>For future reference, "spell
> check" is not a hyphenated word.
>
> Noal

Actually, it's not a word. It's a phrase. And it's a hyphenated
phrase, though many machines vary about their presentation of the term
now that the feature has become popular. Like many things in the
English language, it can be used either way.

It is clear that the previous respondent feels no wrongdoing on his
part for his attacks, and it is clear that we will not agree upon the
nature of such. Thus, I will refrain from responses to the posts of
that person (though I will not dismiss them) as non-abusive responses
to my own are not forthcoming. However, I do still feel that such
abuse indicates a lack upon that person's part (though this is
supposition), so I think it best to satisfy that need. Though I
suggested hobbies before, and think those still good suggestions, in
the interim to the acquisition of such activities I offer the last
word. By all means, respond to this post in a scathing manner, replete
with disparaging comments, to which I will be mute. This will, no
doubt, be a source of satisfaction. Despite the attacks, there was
still the intermittent reasoned response and I am grateful for any
vestige of rational conversation. Though we may not have been
successful, I do wish you good health in your quest to converse with
others here and a good, malicious rant to come.

-- Lemar Johnson

************************************************************************

with Ron and Sue and Peg;

and I got Peggie's leg.

Messages.Author: The Fanboy
Messages.Body:
> What does NR have going for it in constructed? Is the Runner or Corp
> too strong in such a format?

I only participated in one NR constructed event, but the problem was a
common one for early CCGs: Homogeneity.

Every Corp deck I ran against had the same ICE, defended the same
Nodes, installed the same Upgrades, etc. Every Runner deck that went
against me used the same programs, etc. All the decks were identical
to my own.

Deck construction was not a factor in the tournament, and it felt like
we were playing in a sealed event, anyway. The winner won through a
combintation of skill and luck on the run/defend. NOt by building a
superior deck.

Fanboy

Messages.Author: The Fanboy
Messages.Body:
> Sabbat, Settites, Giovanni: evil
> Ravnos: who knows
> Camarilla, Assamites: ok, as far a vampires go (hardly good, but not
> evil).

Gross oversimplification.

Giovanni: Destructive -- their goal is to take over the world by
tearing down the shroud between our world and the land of the dead.
As they have the majority of the Necromantic powers in the world,
they'd be able to rise up and eliminate the problem, thus giving them
a global powerbase surpassing all other forces.

Setites: Evil. They seek to revive a dead God, block out the sun for
all eternity, and create a world in which vampires rule without fear
of their one achille's heel, all the while driving other vampires
further into depravity, giving them control over them.

Sabbat: By our predominately Judeo-Christian morality, undeniably
evil. By their own mindset -- justified. They fight a holy war
against an opponent who serves, in their own mind, the single most
powerful destructive beings in the world (Antedeluvians). They revel
in their inhumane nature initially to undermine the Masquerade in
Camarilla cities, as that creates addtional hardship for their enemy.
As with the Critter: The End series of games, this tactic becomes
habit, and they inevitably spiral downward (upward?) into their
approach to their new existence. Sabbat does a great job of
displaying the grey areas of morality.

Ravnos: Grossly self-serving. They exist to protect their living
family, which is a noble cause, but they do this because they have an
unfounded belief that their family has THE pivotal role in some
undescribed future event. The generally despise all the other
vampires because those vampires have been behind various anti-Romani
programs over the past several centuries. Of course, the Ravnos have
been the most inconsisent clan developed by the tabletop books,
because each new line developer for V:TM seems to want to take them in
a different direction (up to and including Out of the Game, with the
Week of Nightmares of two years back).

Camarilla: Self-serving. They wish to retain their powerbase and not
die. They will eliminate anything that threatens the powerbase or
survival, including Sabbat, independents, whatever.

Assamites: The most noble of the lot -- they feel other vampires (ALL
vampires) are a blight upon the earth, and seek to destroy them.

It is, however, the very nature of vampiric existence that it is
inherently harmful to their food source -- if they kill their prey,
they endanger themselves but grant mercy to thier prey. If they leave
the prey alive, and distort their emotions/perceptions/condition etc,
they maintain their survival, but generally leave a traumatized
individual, who returns to his/her family a fraction of what they were
before, and start a spread of emotional decay.

Fanboy
